#2868. What activating Marcus Bryant, releasing Kindle Vildor means for the Patriots

The New England Patriots remain busy modifying the back end of their roster. After releasing safety Elliott Davison on Monday, they made two other depth moves on Tuesday.

Offensive tackle Marcus Bryant was activated from injured reserve to the active roster, with cornerback Kindle Vildor released. The moves mean that the Patriots still have one open spot on their 53-man team — one considered likely to be used on another player set to come off of IR soon, such as wide receiver Mack Hollins.

What else do Tuesday's moves mean, though? Let's take a closer look at them through a big-picture lens.

During the regular season and obviously depending on each individual situation, every NFL team has the opportunity to bring up to eight players back from its injured reserve list. Entering Tuesday, the Patriots had used two such spots already — one on wide receiver A.J. Brown, who returned in Week 6, and the other on Bryant: he had already been declared as a return candidate back when he was first sent to IR in late August.

This, of course, means that Tuesday's activation did not change the eight-player return count; New England is still on 2-of-8 spots used. What the transaction means, however, is that he has rejoined the 53-man roster just in time before his 21-day activation window came to a close.

As a consequence, the Patriots are now five players deep at offensive tackle:

53-man roster (5): Will Campbell (66 | LT), Morgan Moses (76 | RT), Caleb Lomu (74), Dametrious Crownover (68), Marcus Bryant (52)

Practice squad (1): Lorenz Metz (61 | exempt)

Will Campbell and Morgan Moses are entrenched as the starters, with Caleb Lomu having shown intriguing talent whenever entering the field for one of the two. The fourth spot, meanwhile, will be worth keeping an eye on moving forward. If we base the projection off of training camp and preseason, Bryant would be OT4 — in fact, he even had a case for OT3 after the summer — over rookie Dametrious Crownover.

At the very least, Bryant's return gives New England more flexibility and options up front. That includes using Caleb Lomu as an emergency interior lineman, even though the team clearly would prefer to keep him at tackle as much as possible.

Based on Sunday's game against the Miami Dolphins, Vildor's release comes as a minor surprise. While his 13 snaps on the day exclusively came on special teams, he was part of the game day roster as the fifth cornerback over rookies Karon Prunty and Channing Canada.

In fact, the two youngsters were made healthy scratches. And yet, on Tuesday, it was the veteran — who has so far out-snapped both of them on the season — to be let go.

The why has yet to be determined, although it seems that his status might be directly tied to that of cornerback Carlton Davis, who had missed three games due to a neck injury before returning on Sunday. With Davis back in the lineup, roster flexibility seemingly outweighed the need for a seventh player at the position regardless of experience or résumé.

For the time being, New England's cornerback group therefore now looks like this:

53-man roster (6): Christian Gonzalez (0), Carlton Davis III (7), Marcus Jones (25 | PR), Charles Woods (22), Channing Canada (29), Karon Prunty (21)

Practice squad (1): Al'zillion Hamilton (26)

The expectation is that Vildor could be brought back to the practice squad in the near future. If so, he would naturally become a candidate for game-day elevation again should the circumstances require such a move. Already having used one such elevation earlier in the season, the Patriots can bring him up two more times down the stretch this year.

As noted above, his (or Elliott Davison's, depending on how you look at it) roster spot is meanwhile likely to go to a player currently still on injured reserve. Wide receiver Mack Hollins and fullback Reggie Gilliam are eligible to return to practice this week, while offensive lineman Greg Van Roten is among other players who could make a comeback at any point.

#2867. Adou Thiero ‘trending in the right direction,’ could return from knee injury by end of week

After garnering considerable praise during the offseason and training camp for his development and diligent work, Adou Thiero has unfortunately yet to suit up in the regular season as he deals with swelling in his left knee. But according to head coach JJ Redick, it sounds like the second-year forward is potentially nearing a return.

"He's had some live exposures and I think he's trending in the right direction," Redick told reporters prior to the Los Angeles Lakers' win over the Miami Heat on Monday. "Hopefully by the end of the week he'll be available."

Thiero's latest injury bout marks a turbulent first year and change in the NBA. He missed considerable time as a rookie with swelling in his left knee, which sidelined him for all of preseason and the first 13 games of the regular season, before a sprained MCL in his right knee rendered him unavailable from late December to mid-February.

Fortunately, it sounds like he should be back sooner rather than later; although, swelling in the same knee a year later is undoubtedly concerning.

His point-of-attack defense and general activity, both of which popped at times during the preseason, could help invigorate the Lakers' 18th-ranked defense. They've often struggled to contain the ball and looked overmatched athletically on the perimeter at times. If he can find a reliable role offensively — and playing alongside Luka Dončić and Austin Reaves increases that possibility — Thiero's size and athleticism can remedy some of those issues.

For now, though, the focus is on Thiero becoming fully healthy and returning to the floor. Once he does that, determining whether there's a spot for him in Los Angeles' wing rotation, one that's off to a pretty commendable start through eight games, can enter the conversation.

In the meantime, Los Angeles will keep relying on Ziaire Williams, Matisse Thybulle, Jake LaRavia and Quentin Grimes to hold things down at the forward spots. The Lakers will look for their seventh win of the season when they face the Sacramento Kings inside Golden 1 Center Wednesday night at 7 p.m.

#2866. Vikings mentioned among 'dream trades' for new DL

The Minnesota Vikings are 6-1 and still atop the ultra-competitive NFC North. But after every other division rival won over the weekend, pressure to improve the roster keeps mounting.

Plenty of speculation has surrounded the possibility of the Vikings adding a quarterback or running back to improve an offense that ranks 29th in total yards entering Week 9. But Minnesota may instead opt to bolster a defensive line with several talented yet inexperienced interior players.

One team that could offer interior defensive line help is the Philadelphia Eagles. They have lost six straight games and have already traded center Cam Jurgens, lost RT Lane Johnson to retirement, and are dealing with Jalen Hurts' blood clot issue.

Could the Eagles then make DT Moro Oromo available via trade? And would the Vikings be interested in acquiring the 25-year-old lineman? SI's Connor Orr believes he could be an intriguing addition.

"The Vikings have an excellent fleet of tackles who do exactly what the scheme asks of them, but Ojomo would add a pass-rushing flavor and diversify the array of pressure looks Flores's defense throws," Orr wrote last week. "It's critical for the Vikings to add a showstopping piece as the offense continues to lag. Flores is the most studied coordinator in the league right now and without an evolution midseason, the Vikings could risk losing their biggest advantage. Ojomo is 16th in the NFL in pass-rush win rate among defensive tackles right now."

Per PFF, Ojomo is tied for first among Eagles defenders with 18 pressures. Although he doesn't have any sacks, he accumulated six last season while generating 54 pressures, the second-most on the team.

Ojomo would bring pass-rushing prowess to a defense known for exotic blitzes. He could help offer a change-up where he can cause havoc without always needing to design extra stunts to create those pressures.

Offense still feels like a more pressing need for this team, but there is something to be said for making the strength of the team even stronger. Perhaps Ojomo provides that option.

#2865. AMD has been crushed into earnings. Here’s one way to trade it

Advanced Micro Devices has been under significant pressure leading up to earnings after the close. The stock has been caught in the swings of the AI debate all year, but this most recent leg lower was triggered by a wave of disappointing tech earnings.

A record drop in Alphabet last Thursday was followed by weak results from Amazon, as well as AMD's long-standing CPU rival, Intel. Intel guided fourth-quarter revenue well below consensus and expects the PC slowdown to last through at least the first half of next year. That sent Intel's stock down 29% on Friday, its worst day since the 1970s. Caught in the fallout of Intel and the broader tech sector, AMD fell 10.9% that day and slid another 7.5% Monday.

For the past week, AMD has traded on other companies' news. Now its own numbers get a vote.  AMD's stock reactions have been mixed in recent quarters, sensitive to guidance and high investor expectations. It fell 17% after Q4 2025 results, when a beat and a guide above estimates still underwhelmed some analysts. It rose 18.6% after Q1 2026 results, when it guided about 6.5% above expectations. It fell 7% after Q2 2026 results, when a guide above consensus still fell short of the $14 billion some analysts wanted. That may make direction hard to call, but options let investors build a trade that doesn't have to pick a side.

Based on Monday's close, I'm selling the November 4 425/415 put spread and the 510/520 call spread for a credit of roughly $3.65.

AMD's 30-day implied volatility is elevated going into earnings, closing Monday higher than on about 81% of days over the past year. This means sellers are collecting richer premium than usual. To capture that premium while limiting time beyond the earnings announcement, the trade uses the November 4 weeklies. These contracts imply a move of about 9% through Wednesday, in line with AMD's 8.4% average close-to-close move over its last 10 reports. The short strikes sit at the edges of the expected move, with long strikes $10 away to limit capital at risk going into earnings. This isn't a bet that options are mispricing the move or a directional call. It's a neutral play that aims to profit from the elevated premium that tends to come out after the print.

The trade reaches its maximum profit of $365 if AMD closes between $425 and $510 on Wednesday. Breakevens are $421.35 and $513.65, about 9.7% below and 10.0% above Monday's close, just outside the expected move. The maximum loss of $635 comes if AMD closes below $415 or above $520, roughly 11% in either direction. That has happened in 11 of its last 40 reports, and AMD has had moves as large as 19% in its last four, emphasizing the importance of capping the risk with the long wings.

If AMD finishes between $415 and $425, the short put can be assigned, creating an obligation to buy 100 shares per spread at $425. After the credit, the cost basis is $421.35, or roughly 35% below the Oct. 6 closing high. For investors who like AMD's long-term story, that's a way to end up owning the stock at a discount. A finish between $510 and $520 can assign the short call and leave a short stock position. For investors looking to avoid either risk, consider managing the position before Wednesday's close.

#2864. Fantasy Football Film Room: Buy low on the forgotten Bear; Justin Jefferson is now a boom-or-bust WR2

Fantasy football is inundated with stats and charts (guilty!), but the more context the film provides, the more reliable the data gets. That's why we have a 2.5-hour show called Stats vs. Film every Tuesday at 6 p.m. ET. That show is live — join us in the chat!

This weekly column will look at some of the biggest storylines I picked up by grinding the film.

Previous versions of this column have broken down Colston Loveland's first-read targets and Luther Burden III's exact role in the Bears offense, but Odunze is the forgotten man right now and he feels on the verge of a big game. On Monday Night Football, Odunze had a 4-87-0 line on an 18% target share. That is in line with bye-week WR3/4 value as a baseline, but can it be more?

Odunze is WR3 in 15+ yard receptions (19), only behind Jaxon Smith-Njigba and Tee Higgins. Of the 19 WRs to have at least 11 explosive receptions, Odunze is the lone player to not have a TD on them. What he's done is impossible to do and a very obvious positive regression sign. In this last game, Caleb Williams happened to miss him on a double move go ball heading into halftime that would've been a 50+ yard TD. Odunze has had his fair share of inexcusable drops that should've been scores, but these are the things that should even out moving forward.

The positive plays Monday are what they typically are. He had a 12-personnel dig route on play action where he added a little fake to the outside at the top of his stem for extra separation. These looks are very valuable because there are often 2.5 players in the route, and these throws are often farther down the field. He also had a scramble drill explosive, something that's baked in with Williams being among the best at creating out of structure.

Ben Johnson found a "trick play" that is really easy to execute, but it's enough eye candy for the defense to get lost in the sauce. When D'Andre Swift flips the ball to Caleb, the entire defensive line stops rushing the passer as usual, which gives him extra time and extra space to throw it. The second level zone defenders are also biting and eyeing Swift in the flats more than usual, allowing more space for Odunze to execute his dig route. This is the perfect trick play to me. The risk of ruin is minimized, while still giving the defense something they rarely see.

Quickly on Burden, he played 3 of 21 snaps in heavy personnel. When the Bears established a lead, they went away from 3-WR sets, which is partially explaining the massive splits between halves for Burden this season. He's the WR3 in yards per route in the first half and the WR61 in the second half. When Johnson hasn't isolated him on a first read, the results are worse. That's the reality of a physically dominant yet in-development player. Burden is the WR17 on WR23 usage in games with Caleb this year, so it's no reason to really panic. He's an upside WR2/3 despite the obvious inconsistency.

The backfield is set. Emanuel Wilson was active but didn't play and is on track to be a healthy scratch moving forward, leaving Zach Charbonnet, Jadarian Price and George Holani as the active players. Charbonnet started and played 37% of snaps, leading to 11.6 expected half PPR points (RB22 usage). Price played 48% of snaps, leading to 9.9 expected half PPR points (RB30). Holani played 17%. The trio played on both early and late downs, pass protected, ran routes and carried the ball. It's officially a "let-the-best-man-win" committee, for an organization that held back Kenneth Walker III for years.

So who looked the best? Take a look at this:

Athletically, it's a no contest. Price is so much faster in a straight line and laterally agile. The speed difference is evident on the outside runs, while the lateral ability is easier to see on the cutback runs. That's not the end all, be all, but it absolutely does matter and it's unlikely to change with Charbonnet coming off a February ACL surgery. Price was the one to receive the pitch on a sweep, so the coaching staff obviously agrees.

That said, Price did have two reps where he probably could've done a lot more with the look. One of them was by not giving his center the time to climb to the next level. He instead jammed into a crowded lane, where a more patient and crafty runner would've cut back for a nice gain. The other rep was attempting to bounce it outside of nickel CB Kyler Gordon, when he could've hit his inside shoulder hard for a potential nice gain. Neither were egregious, but the top-end veterans treat them differently.

Charbonnet's runs were more textbook, but there was space to carve out real explosives if he was simply faster. Both of the runs in the video above showcase that glaring flaw. I'd understand it if they'll always value Charbonnet's size and quality decision making in short yardage, but the Seahawks would do well if they continued giving Price a lot of the early down and between the 20s runs to increase their odds of an explosive and to give Price more time on task to develop.

Beyond that, the Seahawks have a very obvious WR depth problem. Jaxon Smith-Njigba is so good that he'll get home regardless, but teams are either straight-up bracketing him or shading a safety over the top of him on most reps. Sam Darnold isn't seeing the field well after the first read, and the depth pass-catchers aren't talented enough to make the reads clearer. It's part of the reason why JSN's role is slightly more underneath this year and very much why Darnold isn't playing nearly as well in 2026. I don't think this is OC Brian Fleury's issue per se, but they need to find another WR at the deadline or find a breakout at RB to counteract this glaring pass-game issue.

The Rams offense has looked a lot different this past month. A lot of that is having zero depth at WR to overcome the Davante Adams injury, but I'm not convinced that's the entire story here.

From Weeks 5-8, Stafford is 1 of 9 on throws with 20+ air yards. The 11% completion percentage and raw completions are obviously alarming but so is the attempt total! He is QB27 in deep attempts on QB6 total attempts during this four-game span.

On tape, Stafford doesn't look fully healthy right now. Some of his sideline and downfield attempts lack his usual zip, and his throwing motion is feeling a little more Philip Rivers-like. He had a sideline completion to TuTu Atwell, but even that one really could've been a score had he led him more. That was more of a line drive that went to his inside shoulder that caused him to hit the brakes a bit. Some of his throws on the move are drifting low and away. And then other throws that are to the intermediate aren't coming with his normal spot-on accuracy.

I wasn't surprised to see Monday's report that his elbow is sore. That's what his throwing motion looks like right now, and the offense being extremely quick-hitting right now is further evidence of just that.

He's fantasy QB16 right now, and I'm not sure if the Rams 3-TE set offense with Puka Nacua working on a 3.4 average depth of target sans Adams is one that's going to lead to massive fantasy days, even if the offense is still moving the ball well. The margins are just a lot tighter in this current offense, and the defense is good enough to keep games on the lower end.

On the Nacua front, he hasn't had a reception of 20+ air yards since Week 4 and has had one target of 15+ air yards in the two most recent games. He's probably not comfortable completely opening up his stride on downfield routes right now, paired with whatever is up with Stafford's elbow. That's OK. He's still the WR3 overall on WR1 usage since returning in Week 4 and is up to 41% targets in the two games without Adams. That'll do.

I still can't believe Lamar Jackson is headed to IR because of a damn thumb injury on the first snap of a showdown with Josh Allen. For Tyler Huntley (turf toe) to also go down is all the more sickening. The Ravens play on Thursday night, so it's too quick to make a move for a Jacoby Brissett or other veteran QB. They'll see what they have with Fagnano again, and it'll be an uphill climb with the Jaguars defense on deck.

Fagnano is a big (6-foot-3, 230 pounds) statue quarterback from UConn, where he finished last year with a 28:1 TD:INT ratio. He went undrafted and has been the QB3 despite not matching up with the Ravens' athletic QB room. He is definitely more of a pocket passer who will struggle to throw on the move or scramble around. That is doubly true now that he's practicing with an ankle brace on. The Declan Doyle offense doesn't need a Lamar Jackson-level athlete to execute, but the margins are tighter, especially behind an offensive line that is in pretty rough shape.

Quickly on that, new center Cam Jurgens has to do a better job of picking up stunts and games. There were too many wasted reps on that alone, and the rest of the right side of the line also had their own issues on one-on-one opportunities. The Ravens really need first-round left guard Vega Ioane back, and he has a chance to return this week.

Fagnano did have a couple of really nice completions to the sideline. They came with anticipation and quality arm talent. That's encouraging in what should be a heavy dropback environment in Week 9 with Jacksonville's defense facing the highest neutral pass rate allowed. Fagnano does look like he can stretch the field horizontally at the very least.

Zay Flowers does a lot of his damage over the middle. It was not Flowers' best work in Week 8. He had a drop on a shallow with room to run. He also fell down on a 3rd-and-8 first-read look before a target was thrown to him. The Bills also bracketed him on another key third down, leading to an incompletion. Fagnano did attempt a big sideline throw to him, but an edge rusher knocked the ball upon release. His lone interception was to Flowers, where he simply stared him down, allowing a zone linebacker to slide his way. My takeaway coming from this game is there is more of a chance for fantasy points for Flowers than what his goose egg would suggest. Fagnano appears to understand the assignment of throwing it to Flowers when he can, but the Jaguars defense will have Travis Hunter and a well-coached defense to squat on these middle-of-the-field throws.

I'd view Flowers as a fantasy starter but more of the WR3 variety than a must start. Here are his splits without Jackson since last year. Please note that last week did fall into the "with" Jackson game. The true split is closer to 13.5 versus 10.5.

Derrick Henry's splits are also problematic. He's the RB28 on RB17 usage this month without Jackson, and his efficiency is night and day depending on if the star QB is out there to threaten defenses himself. I don't trust the OL talent when they simply line up under center, and Henry is far more likely to be phased out due to game script now. He takes the bigger positional tumble in rankings without Jackson and with the Jaguars' dominant run defense. The Ravens have a pathetic team total:

Everyone. The scale I'm using is: Is Justin Jefferson happy? There's no reason he shouldn't be, as very clearly one of the best players in the NFL. Well, right now he's mad and not speaking to the media. Meanwhile, Kevin O'Connell is talking and making pretty direct comments about Kyler Murray: "I thought he made some big-time throws. There were some positives, but there are still some plays we're leaving out there that will help with the overall rhythm of the game. We've gotta continue to find the best way to get him comfortable."

Agree!!! There are some turned down throws beyond his first read, like this one to Jefferson:

Then there are inaccuracies. Murray had a touchdown opportunity up the seam on a correct backside read, but he sailed it. The play below was out of structure, but it's the same result. Sailed. In previous weeks, his intermediate timing-paced routes to Jefferson were missed. Murray has never been considered perfect on these intermediate throws, but this is a step down from his usual for whatever reason.

O'Connell is also on my radar. Even during the Sam Darnold high-flying era, O'Connell left his QB out to dry by asking him to hold onto the ball for downfield concepts without a checkdown available. This is a very difficult offense to run, and it needs an aggressive thrower with stars at receiver to execute. This OL is solid, but it's not elite, making the holding onto the ball part harder.

KOC also doesn't do enough to protect Jefferson when teams are doubling him. The Lions did a great job with Jefferson in Week 8 by playing outside leverage with a CB at the line and sinking a safety to the inside. Jefferson isn't in stacks, in motion, or on the backside of these concepts enough to overcome what is a pretty obvious way to handle this Vikings offense. Murray can't simply throw it up to him in these looks without risk of an interception. The Jordan Addison routes are too often derailed, too. If he played like a first-round WR, then Jefferson wouldn't see these looks nearly as often. This is how Tee Higgins is producing like a top-five receiver in a similar situation.

Jefferson has, by far, the least blame, but he did drop a pass and could've made a highlight touchdown grab up the seam in this past game. He has a 78-855-5 receiving line over his last 17 games for a 50 YPG average. He was at 96 YPG before that. His effort dipped at times throughout this span, but it hasn't been an issue this year. I totally understand if his frustrations start to spill over if this doesn't get corrected. In the meantime, Jefferson has lost his fantasy WR1 label. He's a boom-bust WR2 while the Vikings dip to 31st in passing yards per game on the No. 25 neutral pass rate.

#2863. Phoenix is falling behind, and there’s no room for another slow start

There are plenty of things in life that give people anxiety. For me, it's being late. Or even the threat of being late. Perhaps it's the military man in me, somebody who made the mistake of showing up late to formation during basic training and paid for it in the front-leaning rest position, beads of sweat dripping off my nose and forming a puddle beneath me on the warm pavement at Fort Leonard Wood, Missouri, one June morning. If you're not early, you're late. That's been my mantra ever since.

Unfortunately, that familiar anxiety is beginning to build regarding the Phoenix Suns. This team is 12th in the Western Conference standings after starting 1-4, something we've seen before. At this point last season, the Suns were also 1-4 and were 13th. The difference then is they were only 3.0 games out of first, and due to an odd scheduling start for the Suns and the fact that they have played the fewest games in the NBA, they are 4.5 games back of the top team in the league. That team? The Rockets…

These slow starts create a significant barrier between the Suns and a proverbial train that's already leaving the station, headed toward the postseason. That's right, the Suns are in danger of being late for that train. Anxiety! Because with every passing day and every loss that accumulates, they find themselves falling further and further behind, making it increasingly difficult to hop on board and reach their desired postseason destination.

A season ago, we found ourselves in the same predicament, but the feeling surrounding the team was much different. A big part of that came down to expectations. Nobody really expected the Suns to be a team that could compete at a high level. The prevailing thought was to let the season play out, sell off assets around the trade deadline, and begin building toward the summer of 2026.

Following that 1-4 start, the Suns began putting things together. The sloppy basketball we'd witnessed early in the season became more organized, and the effort that was evident through those first five games finally started translating into wins. I had this to say after they lost 114-113 to the Grizzlies a season ago:

Losing still stings, but this team isn't miles away. The execution needs tightening, and these are the aches that come with learning how to win again.

It's tough to find moral victories in Game 5 when you're sitting at 1–4, but I'll say it anyway. I was entertained. Disappointed, sure. The ending wasn't what anyone wanted. But maybe this year isn't about wins and losses. Maybe it's about how they respond to nights like this.

The feeling this year is different, however. Locally, expectations were higher, even if the national perception remained relatively unchanged. The roster construction was clunky, but you could at least see the vision of what this team wanted to become. Regardless, those expectations change the reality of your situation. While the effort has certainly been present, its consistency has begun to wane, and the execution remains frustratingly inconsistent.

Last season, we could talk ourselves into believing thatDillon Brooks and Jalen Green's absence due to injury was a significant reason for the team's struggles. And perhaps this year, we're doing the same thing with Mark Williams. But the feeling isn't the same. The reality of the situation is slowly sinking in, and it's one in which hope is becoming increasingly difficult to find. This is a team that doesn't control its own draft picks, so finding itself stuck in the middle of the standings is essentially a death sentence.

When you consider the anti-tanking rules that will be in place this year, there's a very real possibility that the Suns could find themselves among the teams with an 8.1% chance of landing the number one overall pick. And how "Suns" would it be for Phoenix to benefit from not being completely horrendous under the league's new draft lottery structure, only to have to hand that pick over to Houston?

Are we there yet? Are we seriously thinking about this already? (I am) When you start 1-4 and look around the standings at the other teams with only one win, seeing the Kings, Nets, Jazz, Bulls, and Bucks alongside you, it's difficult not to get a little frazzled. Because those are the teams that were projected to be bad. It's why we're running to the trade machine trying to find fixes, because you have no room for a down season when there is no benefit to being bad.

I think back to a season ago and the turnaround we witnessed. What the Suns accomplished was impressive, climbing out of 13th place in the Western Conference and playing some incredibly good basketball along the way. For one fleeting night on January 22, 2026, the Suns had fought their way all the way back to the fifth seed in the Western Conference. After starting 1-4, they went 26-13 to reach that point. That is going to be incredibly hard to replicate.

Can this team reproduce any aspect of what we witnessed last year? Can they put together another impressive run that allows them to hop aboard that train headed toward the postseason?

There is hope if you look hard enough. Through their first 5 games a season ago, the Suns had a 120.5 defensive rating (28th) and -9.8 net rating (27th). This season, they are at 124.0 (30th) and -9.8 (25th). After their 1-4 start a season ago, the Suns posted a 112.3 defensive rating (8th) and a +2.1 net rating (13th). It is possible. We've seen it before.

Psst…I'm saying the quiet part out loud…that team can rebound the damn ball…the worst team in rebound percentage last season was the Washington Wizards at 47.1%. The Suns are currently at 45.7%…

We've got a long trip ahead of us, my fellow Suns fans, and we'll spend much of that journey wondering whether this team can recapture any semblance of what it was a season ago. We'll look for solutions in every corner, talking ourselves into the viability of overpaid players like Domantas Sabonis or Dejounte Murray as mediocre saviors. But with so many red flags surrounding the roster construction, it's difficult to shake that familiar feeling of anxiety from being late building in the pit of your stomach.

#2861. Jets sign OL Blake Freeland off Bengals' practice squad

The Jets signed offensive tackle Blake Freeland off the Bengals' practice squad, the team announced Tuesday.

In a corresponding move, the Jets placed offensive lineman Max Mitchell on injured reserve. They also released cornerback Tre Brown from injured reserve.

Freeland joined the Bengals' practice squad after the Colts waived him on Aug. 31. In the preseason, he played 144 offensive snaps over the Colts' three games.

Freeland, who played collegiately at BYU, was selected by Indianapolis in the fourth round of the 2023 draft. He made nine starts as a rookie, while appearing in 15 total games. In 2024, he appeared in eight games and logged 36 special teams snaps and 23 on offense. Freeland missed the entire 2025 season with a fracture in his right leg.

Mitchell was diagnosed with a concussion during a Week 7 practice, and he has missed the past two games. This season, he has played 22 special teams snaps over the first six weeks. Mitchell, who played collegiately at Louisiana, was selected by the Jets in the fourth round of the 2022 draft and has played 51 games.

Brown went on injured reserve on Aug. 30.

#2859. Jim Cramer sees signs of life in tech stocks — but not from the usual winners

CNBC's Jim Cramer said Tuesday that a new group of technology stocks may be emerging as market leaders.

While heavyweights such as Nvidia, Microsoft, Alphabet and Meta have struggled to sustain rallies in recent weeks, other companies are showing signs of strength. That was evident during Tuesday's session as gains from Broadcom and Micron supported the major averages — a sign that investors may be shifting toward a different set of tech winners.

"Tech's trying to make a stand here. It's just not the tech that's led us for the last few years," the "Mad Money" host said.

Cramer pointed to chipmaker Advanced Micro Devices and networking company Arista Networks — both of which reported strong quarterly results after the bell Tuesday — as examples of technology companies that could help lead the sector's recovery. He also highlighted Oracle, whose shares jumped nearly 6% in Tuesday's session.

"I want to believe that non-magnificent tech can lead us," he said. "But I also know that there are concerns we must be aware of before we get too cocky about one session's set of positives."

One concern is growing opposition to data center development, as local communities push back due to fears about rising electricity costs and the facilities' water consumption. He said smaller developers such as Iren, Nebius and CoreWeave could be particularly vulnerable if projects are canceled or forced to relocate, while larger companies like Amazon have more resources to secure alternative locations.

The ongoing war with Iran is another source of uncertainty. Oil prices turned lower Tuesday on hopes there could be progress in U.S.-Iran negotiations. But Cramer cautioned that Wall Street has repeatedly underestimated the risk of further escalation, making it difficult to declare the conflict no longer a threat to markets.

He stopped short of saying that the sector had reached a lasting bottom. After months of failed rebounds, Cramer said he "would like to wait for the crescendo before I commit too much money back into tech."

#2858. Taylor Swift’s Oscar Ambitions Take Center Stage as Travis Kelce Addresses Costly Chiefs Mistakes

Taylor Swift is campaigning for her first Academy Award nomination as her husband, Kansas City Chiefs tight end Travis Kelce, faces criticism following his team's 28-24 loss to the Denver Broncos.

Swift attended an industry screening and Q&A for "Toy Story 5" at Disney's Manhattan offices on Sunday, November 1, as she seeks recognition for her original song, "I Knew It, I Knew You."

Page Six reported that Swift spent time speaking with attendees, signing autographs and taking photographs following the screening.

Meanwhile, Kelce addressed the Chiefs' penalty problems after Kansas City lost a close game against its AFC West rival.

Swift's latest appearance comes months after her work on "Toy Story 5" drew criticism from observers who questioned whether the song was part of a deliberate effort to secure an Academy Award.

At Sunday's screening, attendees described a friendly interaction with the singer.

"She was just adorable with the little kids, hugging each of them," a source told Page Six.

Another attendee said, "She stayed and talked to every single person and allowed selfies and signed autographs."

New York writer Michael Musto also shared details of his interaction with Swift on Instagram.

"Around this time of year, it's Oscar campaigning season and my life gets extra surreal. Today, I got to greet Taylor Swift and couldn't shake-shake-shake-shake-shake off the experience," Musto wrote.

He said Swift complimented his sweater and remembered meeting him previously, describing her as "sweeter than shoofly pie."

Swift is seeking a Best Original Song nomination for "I Knew It, I Knew You." The Academy will announce nominations on January 21, 2027.

During the screening's Q&A, Swift also discussed a longstanding tradition involving her childhood best friend, Abigail Anderson.

Swift revealed that she and Anderson, who have known each other since their teenage years, regularly imitate characters from the 2004 movie "Napoleon Dynamite."

According to Page Six, Swift said they still talk in "Napoleon Dynamite" voices and that their husbands "have to put up with" the habit.

While Swift attended the screening, Kelce and the Chiefs lost 28-24 to the Denver Broncos.

Kansas City committed 11 penalties for 105 yards, including a false start on offensive lineman Jaylon Moore that wiped out a potential game-winning touchdown pass from Patrick Mahomes to Rashee Rice.

Kelce, who has received a penalty in each of his last three games, acknowledged his responsibility for the team's mistakes.

According to The Athletic's Jesse Newell, Kelce briefly stepped away from reporters gathered near his locker before returning with visibly red eyes.

"It's frustrating," Kelce said. "You just can't (expletive) do it, excuse my language. I've got to be better for my teammates, and that sets the tone for a lot of people in this room. Everybody's just gotta up the ante from that."

The tight end also addressed how the Chiefs should respond to the loss.

"You've got to find the positives out of this," Kelce said. "You can't dwell on it. They're a pretty good football team… We showed some fight, a lot of fight. And I can take that out of this."

Mahomes acknowledged the importance of the divisional matchup during his postgame press conference.

"Obviously, it was a big game. I'm not going to hide from that. But, now you're in a dogfight for the division," Mahomes told reporters.

Kansas City will attempt to rebound when it hosts the New York Jets at Arrowhead Stadium in Week 9.

#2857. AI debt fears ease ahead of Oracle, Alphabet and Amazon updates. Here's what to watch.

Fears over artificial intelligence debt have eased after a bout of volatility. But more tests for AI debt are coming.

Oracle holds its Investor Day on Wednesday. And hyperscalers Alphabet and Amazon.com are scheduled to report quarterly results after the market close on Wednesday and Thursday, respectively.

Credit markets are on edge over a flood of AI debt, though fears have eased up a little lately. Meta Platforms' plans for a $95 billion stock offering, announced on Monday, helped bring down its credit-default swap spreads. Those spreads had risen last week when the company reported negative free cash flow in the third quarter. Other CDS spreads had moved higher too, though they have since backed off.

Investors had expected Meta to bring a large bond deal to market shortly after its earnings announcement, said Richard Cheng, head of Nuveen's investment-grade corporate sector team. The fact that it wasn't announced came as a relief.

"Just the absence of the bond deal itself is a direct catalyst for AI-related spread tightening," he said.

A credit spread is the difference in the yield between the corporate bonds and Treasurys of similar maturities. When spreads tighten, it means investors are becoming more confident about the bond issuer.

The market action over the last few days shows that investors are recognizing that "credit fears may have been overblown," said CNBC contributor Paul Meeks, head of technology research at Freedom Capital Markets.

"I expect that these better feelings, maybe not good but better, may continue as companies announce their quarters over the next few weeks."

Still, spreads on CDS remain wider over the past year due to a surge of debt issuance and free cash flows turning negative across the AI space. Meta's CDS spread, for instance, is still up 177% year to date, while Amazon's spread has gained 129%.

"It's not necessarily fundamentals," said CreditSights analyst Jordan Chalfin. "It's more, I'd say, 80% driven by technicals and sentiment."

Alphabet and Amazon pose the next big hurdle for tech bonds as they update their capex plans and free cash flow forecasts. Microsoft's earnings are also due Wednesday, but the company has yet to issue any bonds to pay for its AI spending.

Both Amazon and Alphabet reported negative free cash flow in the second quarter and analysts expect that trend to continue.

Analysts expect Alphabet to report free cash flow of -$2.3 billion while spending $55.2 billion on capital expenditures in the third quarter, according to FactSet consensus estimates. Amazon is expected to report -$9.9 billion in free cash flow against capex of $58.7 billion.

S&P Global Ratings estimated in an August report that the hyperscalers will have negative free operating cash flow in 2026 and 2027.

More critical will be their outlooks, Cheng says. "The singular focus on the investors' minds is really what the capex guidance trajectory looks like across the hyperscaler space."

Meeks believes elevated capex is a sign of strong AI demand. The hyperscalers have "decided that with all the evidence they have — and they have more than you and me — that this is worthwhile spending, and not just worthwhile; it's required," he said.

CreditSights' Chalfin doesn't expect the hyperscalers to announce major new bond issuance around their earnings reports. Oracle's updates may be more critical for credit markets. The company has issued $117 billion in long-term debt and is clinging to an investment-grade credit rating of BBB-, the lowest level of investment grade above junk, according to S&P.

"It's the most important IG tech credit, just given how it's a bit more stressed relative to the A-rated names," he said. "It's trading more like a high-yield credit, even though it's IG, and so there's just a lot of investor concern on that one."

One wrinkle to the AI debt story: balance sheets don't reveal the whole picture. The companies are using complicated off-balance sheet arrangements for data centers and chip financing, and they aren't fully transparent, S&P Global said in a September report.

"There are commitments they are entering into, for example, into data center leases or purchase commitments on chips that aren't necessarily treated as debt," Mark Habib, digital infrastructure sector lead at S&P Global Ratings, said on CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" Monday.

S&P is trying to provide the market with more visibility on those commitments "to give a fuller picture of what kinds of obligations they're actually entering into," he added.

Oracle aside, hyperscaler credit ratings are all comfortably above A levels — reflecting the fact that they have broadly diversified revenue streams, ample coverage for interest payments, and capacity to add leverage if they choose.

Nuveen's Cheng isn't concerned, pointing out that while there has been some credit repricing, there is no credit crisis.

"They continue to have exceptional credit profiles, strong cash generation liquidity," he said of the largest hyperscalers.

"The market is really not concerned about credit quality at this point," Cheng added. "It's really just the trajectory of the capex needs and the supply of debt to fund that. Both of those are pointing in one direction — and that's up."

Correction: This story has been revised to reflect that Oracle's investment-grade credit rating is BBB-, according to S&P. A previous version mischaracterized the company's credit rating.

#2856. Strand bookstore to pay nearly $1.5 million over Covid loan tied to Sen. Wyden's wife

The Strand, the iconic New York City bookstore, agreed to pay nearly $1.5 million in a civil settlement for accepting a Covid government loan that was off-limits because the store is owned by the wife of Oregon Democratic Sen. Ron Wyden, according to the U.S. Attorney's Office in Washington, D.C.

The Strand applied for the $932,350 loan in February 2021 from the Paycheck Protection Program administered by the Small Business Administration, U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro's office said Tuesday.

Store owner Nancy Bass Wyden certified on the loan application that "the spouse of a Member of Congress does not directly or indirectly hold a controlling interest in the applicant," Pirro's office said.

"Ms. Wyden's certification was knowingly and materially false and Strand was not eligible for the second draw loan it received," the office said.

The Strand will pay $1,482,560 to settle the case. There was no determination of liability by the store, Pirro's office said.

The Strand, in a statement, said the store made an "unintentional" mistake in applying for the loan, and said it was unaware at the time the funds were barred to businesses owned by the spouse of a member of Congress.

Bass Wyden's husband, who has served in the Senate for more than 30 years, is a staunch critic of President Donald Trump, who appointed Pirro to the post of top prosecutor in the District of Columbia.

Bass Wyden is the granddaughter of Ben Bass, founder of the Strand, whose flagship store is in Greenwich Village.

Congress authorized the forgivable PPP loans when it passed the Coronavirus Aid, Relief, and Economic Security Act in March 2020.

In December 2020, Congress provided additional funding for the PPP loan program with separate legislation, which "included a prohibition against businesses obtaining second draw PPP funds if a member of Congress or their spouse directly or indirectly held a controlling interest in the PPP loan applicant," Pirro's office said.

In a statement Tuesday, Pirro said, "The Paycheck Protection Program was created to save American jobs, not to enrich those who aren't eligible for taxpayer-funded relief, especially the wife of a U.S. Senator."

Her office noted that the False Claims Act, which the Strand was alleged to have violated, "allows the government to establish liability based on reckless disregard and permits the government to recover more than its actual losses," which is what occurred in this case.

The civil settlement resolved claims brought under a so-called qui tam lawsuit, which allows private whistleblowers to sue on behalf of the U.S. government and receive a portion of any recovery.

The qui tam action in this case was filed by a corporate entity, Blockquote Inc., in U.S. District Court in Washington. Blockquote, whose owners were not disclosed by Pirro's office, will receive a total share of about $148,256 in connection with the settlement.

The docket for Blockquote's lawsuit is sealed from public view.

The Strand, in a statement after CNBC requested comment from the store and Bass Wyden, said the restriction that the store violated was passed by Congress between the first and second rounds of the PPP.

"Unfortunately, the bookstore's accountant and the bank administering the loan were not aware of this change when the second-draw application was processed," the Strand said.

"We stand by the facts: the circumstances arose during an unprecedented and rapidly changing public health emergency, the mistake was unintentional," the store said. "We hope this matter will be viewed objectively and in its proper context, with the understanding that the application of justice should always be fair, impartial, and free from political considerations," the store said.

A spokesman for Sen. Wyden's office said the senator and his wife do not discuss her business, and that he had no involvement in the loan or settlement.

#2855. Snap Count Reactions: Jadarian Price & Zach Charbonnet return, can’t wake Seahawks offense

It's going to be a long week of debate about what exactly ails the Seattle Seahawks after the team was demolished on both sides of the ball against the Chicago Bears on Monday Night Football.

On offense, Zach Charbonnet and Jadarian Price returned to action, while Quenton Nelson took to the field in a Seahawks uniform for the first time since coming over from the Indianapolis Colts. None of that meant anything, and the offense continued to look like trash under first year offensive coordinator Brian Fleury.

At receiver Tory Horton set a career high by playing 43 snaps, but with the ineffectiveness of the offense for most of the game, he did not have much of an impact as he pulled in just three receptions for 26 yards on a half dozen targets.

On defense both Mike Morris and Rylie Mills set or tied their personal career high in defensive snaps played. Morris did so by playing 26 defensive snaps, matching the number of snaps he played against the Los Angeles Rams in the 30-13 to open the 2023 season in his regular season NFL debut. Meanwhile, the 23 snaps played by Mills marked the most of his career, topping the 20 snaps of action he saw in the Week 4 victory over the Los Angeles Chargers.

Drake Thomas also returned to the field for the first time since the Week 5 loss to the San Francisco 49ers, playing 59 snaps, and Dante Fowler continued his unimpressive 2026 performance with just eight defensive snaps.

On special teams Morris once again led the way with 23 snaps, with Brady Russell and Rodney Thomas right behind at 22. At the same time, former starters Emanuel Wilson and Anthony Bradford saw their only action of the night on special teams, as Wilson logged seven snaps and Bradford just three.

And now it's on to the Arizona Cardinals in Week 9, with last place in the NFC West potentially on the line.

#2854. What We Learned from the Spurs win over the Jazz

Somewhere in the second quarter, with the Spurs up one and about to be up more, I realized I wasn't watching the game. I was, instead, watching myself not watch the game, which is a worse hobby and the one I'm apparently best at. The game was fine. The game was exactly what it said on the label: a nondescript tilt between two teams already headed down different tracks. The shine of October basketball had worn off completely and, like summer turning to fall, the Grind had arrived.

As a first quarter blowout turned into a 2nd quarter snoozer, my brain began to wander a bit. I could be anywhere in the world right now. A plastic stool in Hanoi, a bowl of pho, a little light rain. A mountain pass in the Andes, thin air, nobody asking me for a take. Man, I should be reading books. Seeing films. I should be the kind of person whose passport has all those cool stamps in it. This one precious life the universe handed me was unraveling in real time as Ace Bailey stepped into a 25-foot pull-up three to cut the Jazz's deficit to one.

Then Stephon Castle missed a layup and I almost decided to call it a night. It was as annoying as it was unremarkable and I just didn't need it anymore. I reached for the remote and, as I did, Victor Wembanyama, who a minute earlier had similarly flubbed an alley-oop, grabbed the rebound and tipped it back in. Twenty seconds after Bailey's three. No celebration. Barely a facial expression.

I'd love to tell you that's the moment I'd been looking for, but that would be too tidy. What I'd been searching for was a hook. A story, a cause, a catalyst. Anything to hold off the particular ennui of being a fan of a good team. And Wemby wasn't even good last night, not by any stretch. Five of fifteen. Zero for five from three. Five turnovers. He was in that mode he gets in from time to time where he decides the Key to Victory is to simply chuck it.

The Spurs won by 22 anyway, not because of a miracle but because this roster has more than one way to be competent. The Spurs are, mercifully, more than the sum of their parts.

Not that the parts are bad. Quite the contrary. Dylan Harper scored all 17 of his points before the third quarter was half over. Stephon Castle is an animal. De'Aaron Fox looks like the guy we paid for. Tarris Reed continues to grab rebounds in a way that feels like it's going to be important (seven in about seven minutes last night). Every wing combination we've thrown on the court is its own kind of fun.

I mean, look at Harrison Barnes. A man as old as time itself (he's four years younger than me) had an insanely active night. He knocked down threes from 29, 25 and 24 feet, he ran around, he caused trouble. Early in the fourth he got tangled up with Brice Sensabaugh, slid across the floor, got back up, and just stared at him while the refs reviewed it in slow motion. I'm told that clip racked up 140,000 views on the world wide web within about an hour.

The thing about the Grind is that it doesn't have to mean anything, which means that everything within the Grind gets to be exactly what it is. A tip dunk. A well executed outlet pass. An old man staring down Brice Sensabaugh. Like, I didn't come out of the womb craving the Larry O'Brien trophy. I just was at my breakfast table in 1996 watching Michael Jordan dunk on Rik Smits during a SportsCenter rerun, and some part of me said, with zero strategic vision, "Yes. More of that." More of that was the entire ask and, frankly, it still is.

Look at us. You and me. Like I said, we could be anywhere in the world right now, but we're right here with the Spurs and the Jazz on a Monday night in November. The stools in Hanoi will still be there someday, but a precocious superstar, having the worst night of his season, is putting a ball back through the hoop like a child tucking in his stuffed animals for the night.

You don't have to impress some greater importance on a moment like that to make it mean something. You were there. It's a part of you now and you got to live it.

If that isn't special, I don't know what is.

Dylan Harper seems almost casually good at basketball. It's remarkable and breathtaking, these things he's doing, but it also has that effect of seeming effortless when he's casually dismantling another team. In the second quarter he stole the ball and in a blink Vassell was dunking off his pass. In the third, he stole it again and Stephon was finishing an alley-oop before I'd even registered it. He added 8 assists and 7 rebounds on top of all his scoring. I find myself almost taking it for granted at this point, and we've really only started to scratch the surface of what he's capable of. Scary to think about! (For our opponents. For us it's just exceedingly cool and fun.)

I know it's just the Jazz, grain of salt and all that, but I never get tired of seeing the Spurs get out on the break and run. They won fast-break points 26-9, against a Jazz team that turned it over just 11 times, a season low for Utah, so a lot of that was pure rebound-and-go. They also won the paint 52-36 and opened the game on an 18-2 run. Run for days my boys. Grab the ball and never stop running. Only good can come from this. Open looks from three, easy paths to the rim, potential foul trouble for the opponents. Push that pace. Push that pace. PUSH THAT PACE.

This is not how development works and, to be clear, I don't know what I'm talking about, but I absolutely crave Tarris Reed minutes. I want him to become a Sasquatch, Godzilla, King Kong, Loch Ness, Goblin, ghoul and a zombie with no conscience. I want basketballs to fear him checking into the game because they're about to get rebounded to within an inch of their lives.

I love a wire-to-wire win. Next time you hear me complaing about a wire to wire win feel free to come to my house and take an ice cold waterloo out of my fridge as payment for my sins.

I'm a man of all seasons, to be clear, but right now, yes, I am currently in a Waterloo phase of my Sparkling Water career.

There is a particular Black Cherry flavor I've grown fond of and I just can't stay away at this point. It scratches this weird nostalgic part of my brain that yearns for a Blue Sky soda I had in my youth. Do you remember Blue Sky soda?

Yeah, the cans were cool. I don't know. I think I had just never experienced the concept of a soda that existed outside the mainstream world of the Coca-Cola and Pepsi family trees, so when I went on vacation and saw this crazy looking can with a cherry sitting on a cloud it just… broke my brain a little bit and I had to have it.

Who could say? I was six years old. I'd left the summer heat in Texas and woken up the next day in a Colorado mountain town sipping an alien soda from heaven. Maybe it was good, maybe it wasn't, but it stirred something deep in my soul that I think I've been searching for ever since.

And Black Cherry Waterloos scratch that itch for you?

They do. Publix also pretty regularly throws them in Buy One Get Ones for me and who am I to turn down a deal like that.

#2853. CrowdStrike's new kill switch can stop rogue AI agents in their tracks, CEO says

CrowdStrike CEO George Kurtz said Tuesday that the cybersecurity company can now shut down rogue artificial intelligence agents.

CrowdStrike's new kill switch, announced Tuesday at its Fal.Con Europe conference, allows security teams to terminate misbehaving agents, prevent them from restarting and cut off their network access. It is designed to give humans more power over artificial intelligence models and systems, as concerns about how to control agents grow.

"Everyone is building AI agents, but they never had the off button, and now they do," Kurtz told CNBC's Jim Cramer on "Mad Money." "It's going to be an incredibly important part of making sure that AI agents run and operate safely."

The AI Kill Switch, as CrowdStrike calls it, is part of the company's Falcon Guardian platform, which monitors AI agents operating within an organization. The technology, which is available immediately, is aimed at addressing AI safety concerns surrounding the rapid adoption of AI agents.

In September, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for slowing AI development over safety concerns, a position backed by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. Kurtz argued at the time that slowing AI development would not eliminate existing security risks, which he said underscored the need for safeguards as companies deploy autonomous systems.

Kurtz said Tuesday that CrowdStrike's new kill switch represents a significant shift in cybersecurity, which has traditionally focused on protecting companies from external threats. As businesses rely more on AI agents, he argued that security providers must also ensure those systems operate safely within their own organizations.

"Enabling agents to work safely is a massive market opportunity for CrowdStrike," Kurtz said. "We have AI capabilities to prevent these breaches from happening on the outside, and we also have the capabilities to make sure that agents are basically doing what they are instructed to do."

The CEO compared the technology to airbags in cars, arguing that safeguards are necessary even when AI systems are designed to operate correctly.

"If they go outside of those guardrails at runtime, we can kill those agents," he said.

CrowdStrike is seeing growing demand for its security tools as businesses adopt AI. Kurtz pointed to CrowdStrike's partnership with Anthropic to protect its Claude Cowork product: He said enterprise customers had pushed for CrowdStrike's technology to be integrated before they deployed Anthropic's offerings.

"Our customers went to Anthropic and said, 'We need CrowdStrike before we can deploy AI,'" Kurtz said. "I think it says volumes that customers would not roll out AI without CrowdStrike."

Shares of CrowdStrike closed at a record high of $278.86 on Oct. 6 but have since fallen about 12% as tech stocks struggled in October and into November.

#2852. Predators' Juuse Saros inspired by 'big brother' Pekka Rinne in win vs Hurricanes

With the soon-to-be Hockey Hall of Fame goaltender looking on, the Nashville Predators beat the Carolina Hurricanes 4-1 at Bridgestone Arena on Nov. 3.

And Rinne's main pupil, goaltender Juuse Saros, played sensational in net for the Predators.

"His big brother was here," captain Roman Josi said after the win, which was the second straight for the Predators (6-4-5, 17 points).

Saros made 29 saves, including 12 in the third period, to improve to 4-3-4 on the season. According to Money Puck, he saved 2.56 goals above expected, holding the Hurricanes (12-3-2) to one goal on 3.56 expected goals.

"He made so many amazing saves tonight and he's been doing it all year," Josi added. "It's pretty cool for all of us to have (Rinne) in the building."

Before the game, Rinne was honored with a ceremonial puck drop and a video tribute. On Nov. 9, Rinne will be inducted into the Hockey Hall of Fame alongside Patrice Bergeron, Carey Price, Cindy Curley, Keith Tkachuk and Brian Burke. Rinne will be the second Predators player to enter the Hall, joining defenseman Shea Weber (2025).

The Predators' most decorated goaltender, Rinne is the all-time franchise leader in wins (369), shutouts (60), and playoff wins (45). Before he retired in 2021, Rinne helped mentor a young Saros, developing him into the team's starting goaltender.

Since his NHL debut in 2016, Saros leads Nashville in wins (233) and shutouts (27).

"(Rinne) is one of the all-time best goalies and human beings," coach Andrew Brunette said. "When he's around (Josi) and (Forsberg) and (Saros), the guys that played with him, it just kind of uplifts them."

On that point, Josi and Forsberg also played well in the win: Josi scored a goal and assist, and Forsberg had two assists, including one on Josi's goal.

"It's almost like they don't want to let (Rinne) down, which is pretty cool to see," Brunette added. "The impact that (Rinne) has on this organization, that's why he's a Hall of Famer."

Next up, the Predators visit the Colorado Avalanche on Nov. 5 (7 p.m. CT, ESPN+).

#2851. 49ers trade targets: 4 players San Francisco could pursue at NFL trade deadline

The San Francisco 49ers have an opportunity to improve their roster ahead of the league's trade deadline on Nov. 10.

The Niners return from the bye week ready to bring their former defensive lineman DeForest Buckner back into the fold after completing a trade with the Indianapolis Colts, bringing the 32-year-old back to the Bay Area.

The deal for Buckner was just a start; San Francisco isn't expected to be done yet. The 49ers' main concern is depth and making sure they have enough bodies to make it through the regular season and into the postseason.

The 49ers are 6-1 but have dealt with a ton of injuries throughout the year, mainly at defensive line and wide receiver. Those are areas where San Francisco could use more depth.

TRADE GRADES: Who won the DeForest Buckner trade?

The Niners tried to bring back former receiver Jauan Jennings in a trade with the Minnesota Vikings, but Jennings denied the trade.

Receivers that have been out for the 49ers include Ricky Pearsall, De'Zhaun Stribling, DeMarcus Robinson and tight end Jake Tonges. Deebo Samuel Sr. is expected to be ready to go after sitting with a right hamstring injury. KhaDarel Hodge was signed to the 49ers' practice squad and the 32-year-old wide receiver might have a chance to play against the Las Vegas Raiders on Nov. 9.

49ers receiver Brandon Aiyuk hired a new agent, bringing Drew Rosenhaus on his team in an attempt to return to the NFL. Still, San Francisco is likely not an option.

Although things aren't terrible on the defensive side of the ball, San Francisco could use upgrades defensively, at least more help in their pass rush and on the edge.

The 49ers defense is 20th in sacks and 27th in takeaways, including 29th in interceptions and 19th in forced fumbles. San Francisco's run defense allows 89 yards per game, the 5th-fewest in the league. They're third in total rush yards with 623 through 7 games. They've allowed the fewest rushing touchdowns, three.

Still, the injuries the 49ers have experienced still affect them. They've been dealt injuries to Nick Bosa, Alfred Collins, C.J. West, Sam Okuayinonu, Mikail Kamara and Andrew Farmer II. All have missed time going in and out of the lineup. The 49ers only recently got Mykel Williams back from an ACL injury.

Still, the 49ers may consider a move ahead of the Nov. 10 deadline. Who could they target if they keep buying? Here's a look at the top trade options San Francisco could pursue.

The 49ers need a WR and Jaguars wide receiver Brian Thomas Jr. could use a fresh start after a slow start to the season. In his third season, Thomas, through seven games, has recorded 10 receptions, 117 yards and two touchdowns. He averages 11.7 yards per catch.

He earned a Pro Bowl selection during his rookie year in 2024 for season stats of 87 catches, 1,282 yards and 10 touchdowns in 17 games. Then he had a sophomore slump. He played 14 games and only tallied 48 catches, 707 yards and two touchdowns.

San Francisco needs more young weapons in their aging WR room after all the injuries. Thomas would be a dream to team up with Mike Evans, Deebo Samuel and tight end George Kittle.

Khalil Mack is 35 and was the 5th overall pick selected by the then-Oakland Raiders in the 2014 NFL Draft. The former NFL Defensive Player of the Year is older but can still provide a spark as a vet. Mack built his career as a pass rusher, compiling 116 career sacks and ranking seventh all-time among active players.

Mack has done just about everything in the NFL, except win a Super Bowl. He was the 2016 Defensive Player of the Year, a nine-time Pro Bowl selection and a three-time All-Pro linebacker. He might thrive in a role where he can win a coveted Super Bowl ring.

The Los Angeles Chargers are winless. Mack seems to be nearing the end of his career but could get a boost in a winning situation. Mack could add more depth to the 49ers' defensive front. He has three sacks and 11 tackles this season. His snaps might be limited, but he could be a force rushing the passer and even spell Nick Bosa when he returns.

Will McDonald IV could be the power punch on the edge that the 49ers are looking for. He plays a complementary role in New York, but he can be effective when he sees snaps. McDonald is a 6-foot-4, 245-pound pass rusher who has 23.5 career sacks and four forced fumbles in 54 games.

That kind of addition could give San Francisco another weapon on the line as they look to fill the void left by injuries. McDonald possesses a skill set that would complement the 49ers' existing defensive line with a healthy Keion White, Gracen Halton, Osa Odighizuwa, Romello Height and Mykel Williams.

So far in 2026, he has three sacks and seven total tackles.

The 49ers already knocked on the Colts' door to make a trade; why not do it again? San Francisco needs wide receivers and Indianapolis is apparently undergoing a fire sale. The 49ers would do themselves a favor by going after Josh Downs. The 25-year-old wide receiver has 30 catches, 330 receiving yards and one touchdown this season.

He would give the Niners another fresh look at wideout lining up predominantly in the slot. He's shifty in his cuts and is another QB-friendly target. He would be a solid addition for San Francisco as they ease back Mike Evans and Deebo Samuel from injury. The 49ers could await for their rookie De'Zhaun Stribling to return but in the meantime, a trade would mean they don't have to rush him back, or put additional pressure on him to perform.

#2850. Former Arizona wing Dalen Terry signs with Thunder

Dalen Terry is on an NBA roster after starting the season on the sidelines.

In 218 career games, Terry is averaging 3.5 points, 1.7 rebounds, 1.2 assists and o.5 steals per game.

The 6-foot-6 Terry arrives in Oklahoma City following injuries to the Thunder's Jalen Williams and Cason Wallace. The Thunder are also without big man Chet Holmgren for at least two months.

Terry was drafted 18th overall by Chicago in the 2022 NBA Draft. He comes the 17th former Arizona basketball player to be on an NBA team this season, the third-most of any school behind Kentucky and Duke.

#2849. Binance co-CEO Richard Teng says hackers used fake job interviews, AI tool to steal $6.3 billion in crypto

Binance said hackers used fake job interviews, malicious software and compromised internal AI tools to infiltrate its wallet infrastructure, leading to the record-breaking Oct. 29 cyberattack that resulted in more than $6 billion in assets being stolen from the world's largest crypto exchange.

The attackers "spent months building their way in," Binance co-CEO Richard Teng told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" Tuesday, rejecting suggestions that there was a single point of failure through one employee's laptop.

"In June, [the attackers] set up a fake version of a developer tool and lured one of our engineers to install that," he added. "In September they posed as recruiters and ran a series of job interviews with another engineer, and that ended up in a coding exercise that contained hidden malware designed to evade security ... from there they moved violently through our internal AI tools and obtain[ed] access that breach[ed] the system that authorized our wallet transaction."

He also said Binance has replenished 98% of $6.34 billion in affected assets, and that it is still in the process of purchasing outstanding, more illiquid assets.

Teng himself did not attribute the attack to North Korea but acknowledged that the FBI has linked it to North Korean hackers tied to the TraderTraitor group.

Preparations for the attack began in June, when a Binance Wallet DevOps engineer downloaded a tampered Homebrew installation "to install a popular AI coding tool after searching for it on a search engine," according to a security report published by Binance Tuesday. It said it detected the suspicious activity, replaced the engineer's device and rotated credentials as a precaution, but that by then the employee's "role and his related colleagues on our wallet infrastructure team was exposed to the hacker."

As Binance works to recover from the incident, it has temporarily restricted certain withdrawals, pledged to cover all customer losses and tapped its own reserves to replenish affected assets. Binance and industry partners including Tether, Circle and Ripple have reportedly frozen about $3 billion in assets, though some stolen funds continue to move through laundered channels. Coinbase blocked transfers to compromised wallets and offered Binance direct assistance.

Although the incident represents a significant security breach, Binance maintains that it remains financially sound and focused on identifying the vulnerability, recovering remaining funds and preventing another attack.

The hack sparked a sharp but short-lived hit to confidence across crypto markets, especially compared with previous failures at major exchanges. Investors are now watching whether Binance can fully restore confidence in centralized exchanges.

As of Tuesday Binance has rebuilt the affected wallet system and internal AI tool, replaced compromised devices, decommissioned credentials and tokens associated with the affected engineers and expanded security scans across employee devices, Teng told "Squawk on the Street."

"We're also getting an independent expert to review everything that we have done, and we'll keep strengthening our defenses as the investigation continues," Teng said. "We're working around the clock with law enforcement agencies and with industry partners to trace and freeze the stolen funds for that front."

#2848. Predators' Juuse Saros inspired by 'big brother' Pekka Rinne in win vs Hurricanes

With the soon-to-be Hockey Hall of Fame goaltender looking on, the Nashville Predators beat the Carolina Hurricanes 4-1 at Bridgestone Arena on Nov. 3.

And Rinne's main pupil, goaltender Juuse Saros, played sensational in net for the Predators.

"His big brother was here," captain Roman Josi said after the win, which was the second straight for the Predators (6-4-5, 17 points).

Saros made 29 saves, including 12 in the third period, to improve to 4-3-4 on the season. According to Money Puck, he saved 2.56 goals above expected, holding the Hurricanes (12-3-2) to one goal on 3.56 expected goals.

Rinne will be the second Predators player to enter the Hall, joining defenseman Shea Weber (2025).

The Predators' most decorated goaltender, Rinne is the all-time franchise leader in wins (369), shutouts (60), and playoff wins (45). Before he retired in 2021, Rinne helped mentor a young Saros, developing him into the team's starting goaltender.

Since his NHL debut in 2016, Saros leads Nashville in wins (233) and shutouts (27).

"(Rinne) is one of the all-time best goalies and human beings," coach Andrew Brunette said. "When he's around (Josi) and (Forsberg) and (Saros), the guys that played with him, it just kind of uplifts them."

#2847. AMD stock jumps 8% on earnings as data center revenue nearly doubles

Advanced Micro Devices reported third-quarter earnings on Tuesday that beat Wall Street's expectations, with revenue jumping 45% and data center sales nearly doubling from a year earlier. The stock was up 8% in extended trading.

Here's how the chipmaker did versus LSEG consensus estimates for the quarter:

Revenue increased from $9.25 billion a year earlier, AMD said in a statement. Neoclouds like CoreWeave and Nebius rallied earlier Tuesday and remained higher after AMD reported results.

CEO Lisa Su said on the earnings call that she expects server revenue to double year over year in 2027 and data center AI growth to accelerate even faster than the company had projected 90 days ago. The company expects data center to drive the majority of its revenue and earnings growth.

"We have worked across our supply chain to secure the wafers, substrates, advanced packaging, memory, and other key components needed to support much higher growth next year," Su said on the earnings call.

AMD's report comes days after Intel disclosed similar data center growth, with revenue in that segment up 78% in the third quarter. But Intel's stock plummeted 29% on Friday over concerns about weak guidance and Intel's ability to meet demand.

The data center unit makes up the majority of AMD's business, accounting for 64% of overall revenue, up from 47% a year ago.

After years spent chasing Nvidia in the market for artificial intelligence graphics processing units, or GPUs, AMD's central processing units, or CPUs, are experiencing a major resurgence with the rise of agentic AI apps like Meta's Muse. AMD's server CPUs are key for agentic apps because they power virtual machines and can run for hours on their own. Demand from agentic AI boosted AMD shares to a record in October.

"Adoption is just starting, and we expect demand to grow sharply as agents are deployed more broadly and take on more complex work," Su said on the earnings call with analysts.

AMD's stock is up about 125% this year, but it saw three consecutive days of losses before rallying on Tuesday amid an industrywide sell-off tied to fears about overspending on AI.

AMD is also a major player in the weakening PC market, which Intel blamed for its poor outlook last week. AMD and Intel are the largest makers of traditional x86 processors that power many laptops and desktops, while other laptops rely on Arm-based processors from the likes of Qualcomm and Apple.

Global PC shipments declined 4% in the second quarter from a year earlier due to soaring costs for memory and other components, according to Counterpoint Research.

AMD reports PC chip sales in a segment combined with gaming chips. Revenue in that business fell 8% from a year earlier to $3.7 billion. Gaming revenue was down 40% from a year ago.

For the fourth quarter, AMD said it expects about $17 billion in revenue, beating the $16.2 billion average analyst estimate, according to LSEG. AMD sees its gross margin for the quarter coming in at 55%, slightly below the average estimate of 55.3%, according to StreetAccount.

AMD also sells data center GPUs and full rack-scale systems called Helios that compete directly with Nvidia's Grace Blackwell and Vera Rubin systems. Meta, Microsoft, Anthropic, OpenAI, and Oracle are all beginning to use AMD Helios in their data centers. Meta said last week that its Helios racks are up and running, and AMD agreed to invest $1 billion in Meta's equity offering.

AMD has also committed to investing up to $5 billion in Anthropic, which unveiled its highly anticipated prospectus last week as it inches closer to a potentially historic initial public offering.

During a visit to Taiwan in October, Su said she plans to "substantially increase our supply in 2027." Su and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang have both made multiple trips to Taiwan and South Korea this year, holding meetings with key suppliers like Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company and memory leaders SK Hynix and Samsung.

In September, AMD said it would acquire World Labs for $8.2 billion in an all-stock deal. The San Francisco-based AI lab, founded by industry pioneer Fei-Fei Li, is developing a so-called world model that simulates 3D environments to aid in developing robots and other physically grounded AI applications.

St. Xavier and Sycamore faced each other in the state semifinals, with the Bombers passing the Aviators in a 19-14 win. St. Xavier focused on shutting down Sycamore's star Ciaran Skinner with double-teams on defense, then using a balanced offensive attack that saw six Bombers score goals.

Senior goalie Lucas Mijares made multiple impressive saves in the first half to keep the Bombers competitive with the Golden Bears.

It was the third consecutive appearance in the state semifinals for St. Xavier, but just its first trip to the finals since 2016. The Bombers' season wrapped up at 22-16-1 overall, recording a third-place finish at the Ohio Cup and a top-eight placement at Philadelphia's Beast of the East Tournament.

Sycamore, who entered the tournament as the No. 7 seed, made a statement win in the quarterfinals. The Aviators knocked off defending champions St. Charles, who had only lost three times in 2026, in a 9-6 battle. Senior Colin McAllister earned a full line in the contest, while senior David Parker was the unsung hero in denying the Cardinals' 2-meter player any space to initiate the offense.

Following their loss to St. Xavier in the semis, Sycamore knew it had a physical matchup with Thomas Worthington coming up. After a back-and-forth three quarters, the physicality got the better of Thomas Worthington as two key players were fouled out or ejected. Sycamore won the final quarter by four goals, winning the match 16-12.

Sycamore senior Ciaran Skinner, a first-team All-Ohio selection, made history in the state tournament. His 163 goals set a new single-season goal record, eclipsing the previous mark of 156. He scored 18 goals over four games in the tournament, also adding six assists, 23 steals, and 14 ejections drawn.
