#2813. Player Grades: Knicks 103, Nets 90

For three quarters Monday night, the Knicks looked like they might actually lose to the Nets. The Nets? The last place Nets? While we might get apoplectic, the champs seemed unconcerned about falling behind. When they finally flipped the switch, they turned a 79–75 deficit into a 103–90 win, outscoring Brooklyn 28–11 in the fourth at the Garden. That's 15 straight wins against the neighbors. Landry Shamet did a lot of the work to make it so.

22 points (6–8 FG, 4–6 3PT, 6–6 FT), 1 rebound, 1 assist in 30 minutes

On a night when the starters happily hurled threes like pre-teens playing Pop Shot, Shamet sank a steady four of six, plus every free throw he took. His season-high 22 kept the Knicks in it long enough for the rest of them to wake up.

While the Knicks spun their wheels in third-quarter mud, Josh Hart collected his fourth foul with a lotta game remaining. Shamet replaced him at 8:44 and scored six points on perfect shooting from downtown. The first, at 2:26, cut Brooklyn's lead to a single point; the second, with a minute left, made it 77-75. According to Basketball Reference, he had a team-high game score of 19.4. Pretty good for a sub.

8 points (3–6 FG, 2–5 3PT), 6 rebounds, 7 assists, 3 steals in 27 minutes (+22)

Hart had a crooked finger in just about everything that made the fourth quarter exciting. In that final frame, he hit a Kolek-assisted three to pull the Knicks within one, then assisted on back-to-back Anunoby threes and a Kolek layup (everybody seems to enjoy playing with Tyler, don't they?). Josh intercepted a Julius Randle pass and took it the other way for a layup. His grade suffers for taking just six shots and collecting six fouls, but maybe he deserves a little more love for being a team high +22?

18 points (4–10 FG, 3–7 3PT, 7–8 FT), 4 rebounds, 2 assists, 2 steals in 38 minutes

OG played 38 minutes, got to the line eight times, and hit back-to-back threes in the fourth when the Knicks finally started to put Brooklyn away. Seven free throws will do a lot for a night when only four shots fall from the floor. Give credit to his stamina: after bumping bodies with that bull Julius Randle all night, he still had gas in the tank to help his team in the fourth. He hit the go-ahead three at 10:29 and another bomb 28 seconds later to make it 84–79. He also set up Clarkson's transition three. Loses points for still struggling to finish at the rim.

11 points (4–11 FG, 1–4 3PT), 16 rebounds, 5 assists in 35 minutes

A weird game for Karl-Anthony. He had double-digit rebounds in the first half, but zero points. After intermission, he scraped together 11 points with much more aggressive drives to the rim. As New York rallied in the fourth, he banked in a short fadeaway, grabbed three defensive boards, and found Landry Shamet for the Knicks' final basket. His back up, Andre Drummond, grabbed nine boards in his 13 minutes, but dividing the workload between the pair is unsustainable. James Wiseman is glued to the bench. Leon, what's your move?

19 points (6–16 FG, 4–11 3PT, 3–6 FT), 2 rebounds, 6 assists in 33.5 minutes

Four threes and six assists are dandy, but missing half his free-throws and ten field goal attempts had us a little worried. He's been mostly automatic since coming to New York, so forgive us for jumping to conclusions like: maybe he should spend less time doing extracurricular activities and more in the gym? He started off the game great, making 3-of-4 from deep, but then disappeared for a while.

7 points (3–5 FG, 1–2 3PT) in 11 minutes (+17)

Some guys can do a lot in 11 minutes. Clarkson squeezed seven points into his sliver of time (entirely in the second half) and was still a +17. As the fourth quarter started, a game that had been a nuisance all night was finally starting to break open. Jordan blocked Nolan Traoré's layup and hit a transition three seven seconds later to push the lead to 10. He added a floater at 4:00 to keep the momentum going. He loses a point for collecting two fouls and a technical foul in the span of a minute during the third period, which didn't help matters while the team was flailing.

After the game, coach Mike Brown offered high praise for the vet. "I've been around some good teammates when it comes to players. He's gotta be the best. He's the definition of ultimate pro," he said. "You have a veteran that's been there, done that, and he's willing to accept the role that most guys wouldn't accept […]. And he's willing to accept it… and still try to uplift everybody and connect everybody while he's going through what he's going through. That's the ultimate team player."

6 points (2–4 FG, 2–4 3PT), 1 rebound, 2 assists in 16.5 minutes

Deuce hit two of four from deep and added a couple of assists. A decent shift on a night when the Knicks could've used a few more of those. Two steals is great. Four shots in almost 17 minutes seems insufficient, however.

6 points (1–7 FG, 0–2 3PT, 4–4 FT), 2 rebounds in 16 minutes (−11)

Hoo boy. Bridges made one shot from the floor and did little on defense to make up for it. The Knicks lost his 16 minutes by 11 points, the worst mark in the rotation. At least he got to the foul line for the first time after six games.

It's perhaps too soon to sound the panic alarm, but he has shot 16 of 52 for the season. Mike Brown has taken notice. He ended Kal's night after just a few minutes into the third quarter, and when he sent the starters back at the end of the game, Shamet took Bridges' spot.

The Knicks got away with three quarters of sleepwalking because Shamet kept them close and Hart, OG, and the bench gave them life in the fourth. Next up are the Bulls on Wednesday. In their first meeting of the season, last week, the Knicks won but needed 48 points from the bench to bail them out. Do we see a trend emerging?

#2809. Santoli: AI bull market almost surely needs tech stocks to recover to keep advancing

The road to bull-market glory does not run through Walmart and Berkshire Hathaway and Eli Lilly.

There's been a virtual buying panic in traditionally defensive, high-quality stocks over the past few weeks, a near-equal-and-opposite offset to the selling pressure in semiconductors and AI-build-out spenders. The three stocks above — the only members of the $1 trillion market-cap club not in Big Tech – have collectively added $550 billion in market value in the past month, almost making up for what Alphabet has lost.

The Nasdaq-100 and the S&P 500 Low Volatility ETF (SPLV) are rushing toward one another in a satisfying picture of symmetry that nonetheless reflects an almost comical level of tactical rotation executed by an investment community accustomed to playing one factor against another.

While this to-and-fro has so far protected the S&P 500 as a whole from an appreciable setback for months, it has left it stymied around levels that date back to May — before we got two earnings-reporting seasons showing 30% annual profit growth.

A week ago here, I suggested the AI theme was nearing a make-or-break moment to stage a recovery or risk surrendering its leadership status and destabilizing the broader market. Thus far, this trade has failed to respond to moderate oversold conditions or a run of cosmetically strong hyperscaler quarterly results, further loosening its grip on the benefit of the doubt.

In stressed markets undergoing soul-searching about the long-term bullish thesis, prices often need to travel further to find buyers with conviction while the market action must disappoint dip-buyers to extinguish complacency. Hard to know if we're there, but presumably we're now closer.

The Nasdaq-100 closed Monday right at its 200-day moving average, off almost 11% from its record high. After an enervating failed Monday-morning bounce attempt, the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index finished down another 3.8% and settled under the late-July low that was set as the Situational Awareness hedge fund was finished liquidating.

"Markets did not get the memo that bearish seasonal pressure typically subsides in mid-October and instead ended the month with some of the most acute selling pressure that has been realized during the late-summer/early-fall period," notes JPMorgan technical strategist Jason Hunter. He's advising clients to remain on the defensive "until we see clear evidence of a bottoming process on the charts or until there are clear signs of capitulation."

This is a time-tested playbook, though many a sharp market pullback has ended without what would qualify as unqualified capitulation.

The market action is winning some plaudits for the way non-tech stocks have held up better, many groups benefiting from the "quality" rotation while abandoned consumer cyclicals get a reprieve from easing oil prices and the slide in the 10-year Treasury yield back below 5%.

This gives active managers plenty to do in playing against a highly concentrated and tech-dependent S&P 500. But I'll continue to argue that the bull market built on the AI story will almost surely need the AI story to get back on track to keep advancing. A prolonged period when the equal-weight S&P 500 outperforms the market-cap-weighted version is otherwise known – usually – as a bear market.

The AI-related stocks' weighting in the S&P 500 is off the highs but remains near 45%, according to Morgan Stanley.

As the chart shows, AI has wobbled relative to the rest of the market during this uptrend before reasserting itself.  But there's a trickier element to the current gut check: In prior phases of the buildout, the key limiting bottleneck gave investors something to buy in order to exploit it.

The initial scarcity of GPUs meant to own Nvidia above all else from 2023 through 2024. When cloud capacity, power and cooling were found to be the crucial scarce resources, hyperscaler stocks worked and the AI-adjacent industrials were drastically revalued. Then memory emerged as the chokepoint and Micron and Sandisk went stratospheric.

Now, as Nvidia's Jensen Huang has said, capital is the constraint and that not only leaves no asset to buy, but it raises the cost of capital broadly as the mega-caps go free-cash-flow-negative.

Overlapping feedback loops and scrambled correlations across the markets and the real economy have further sapped investor conviction. Treasury yields no longer move with oil but largely with AI-capex sentiment, with both in retreat lately. AI-stock setbacks also mute inflation momentum and the equity wealth effect, meaning fewer Federal Reserve rate hikes are anticipated now versus a month ago.

This all probably sounds like an elaborate trap, and it has become one for the previously crowded trades. Could this reflect the end game for the AI-exuberance market chapter, which as I keep pointing out peaked around the SpaceX IPO in June? Impossible to say for sure, but if it were, I'm not sure things would look much different to this point.

But I don't want to dismiss the possibility that a lot of the known challenges are largely reflected in prices.

I argued in August that we should assume the valuation peak for this cycle was in. We've now retrenched to a forward P/E of 18.5 on the S&P 500 from 23 a year ago and the Nasdaq-100 at 20x is at the slimmest premium to the S&P 500 valuation in nine years. I'm on board with the idea that the market is telling us companies are now "over-earning," but if nothing else there is less valuation risk now than in recent months.

Sentiment toward AI stocks is in the dumps. Funds' positioning in tech has retreated below neutral. Important trading lows this year have happened near the turn of the month on March 30 and July 29, and the Nasdaq-100's relative-strength reading is exactly as oversold as it was at those turns.

So, stay alert for possible relief bounces that could evolve into something more consequential if indeed the midterm elections pass in a way that allows traders to unclench a bit into the year's home stretch.

John Kolovos of Macro Risk Advisors on the latest reading: "Similar to valuation, sentiment is not a timing tool, but it is getting harder and harder to find any bulls, as a near-perfect storm of tight financial conditions is being met with tech earnings that have gone from bad to worse in the blink of an eye."

-Another good big-picture conversation on the practical business and investment implications of the next phase of AI proliferation on Patrick O'Shaughnessy's Invest Like the Best podcast, this one with investor Cliff Sosin. His comparison of AI infrastructure economics to internet connectivity providers and his argument for how most of the productivity boost will go toward "consumer surplus" rather than corporate profits are particularly interesting.

-For my birthday Monday, my colleague and friend Sara Eisen wondered how I would write a birthday message to myself. I immediately regretted suggesting she ask ChatGPT, which generated this credible and somewhat embarrassing result:

"Another year older, though the longer-term trend remains constructive. Some modest deterioration in the underlying internals, perhaps, but nothing that suggests a decisive breakdown.

"The candles on the cake are approaching historically elevated levels, though valuation concerns have persisted for years without derailing the advance. At this stage, the key question isn't whether I've gotten older — that's largely priced in — but whether the wisdom gains can continue to offset the inevitable compression in energy multiples.

"For now, I'm maintaining a cautiously optimistic outlook, with upside optionality, downside support from family and friends, and no immediate need for Fed intervention. Happy birthday to me. The secular bull market remains intact."

The stampede into perceived defensive stocks has been a crucial driver of Apple shares' massive outperformance over the Nasdaq-100 since the AI-capex agita flared up months ago. Apple heading into Monday's earnings report had outperformed the Nasdaq-100 by nearly 20 percentage points over the prior six months.

Its singular refusal to join the aggressive spending binge to build AI capacity preserved its free cash flow and made it the perfect counterweight to the capex trade, while inflating Apple's valuation to a 15-year high.

But its advantage in free-cash-flow yield has now narrowed, thanks to its stock-price gains and the collapse of peer shares.

#2805. Cleveland Browns: Run defense is scary. And not in a good way.

The Cleveland Browns faced some questions on the defensive side of the ball heading into the 2026 season.

The biggest concern was how Mike Rutenberg would handle being a defensive coordinator for the first time, especially since he was taking over for the highly regarded Jim Schwartz, who had been in charge of Cleveland's defense for the past three seasons.

Outside of a Week 1 disaster against Jacksonville, the defense has been one of the consistent bright spots in Cleveland's 5-3 start.

One area that has been an issue, however, is the run defense, which has been up and down through eight games.

When the run defense has been good, it's been pretty good, as the Browns held Carolina, Baltimore, and Pittsburgh (in the first meeting) all under 100 rushing yards.

But when it has been bad, it has been bad and steadily getting worse. Cleveland allowed an average of 132.2 rushing yards to Jacksonville, Tampa Bay, and the New York Jets. But in the last two games, Tennessee rushed for 141 yards, while the Steelers piled up 200 rushing yards in Sunday's rematch.

What's worse, after allowing just one rushing touchdown in the first six games, the Browns have allowed a total of six in just the past two games.

So what is going on? Is it a lack of effort? Are opposing offenses figuring out the defense? Or is the defense wearing down from having to carry so much of the burden while the offense has struggled?

According to head coach Todd Monken, it is a combination of the last two items:

"I don't see it as a mindset. Our guys play their rear ends off – they're physical. Every game's different, every week is different. We've got to play better on the road. We've got to play from in front. That will give us a chance to play the run better and force them to make calls. But there are a number of things we're going to have to do to change, because we're going to continue to see those types of runs, those schematic runs against the attack style, and where we go from here.

"We weren't at our best the last couple of weeks in stopping the run. All right, now what? What are we going to do to stop the run? What are we going to do to put ourselves in a position where we're always trying to make a team one-dimensional, no doubt, but where we can mitigate those long plays."

It is worth pointing out that, despite the hand-wringing over Schwartz leaving the team, the Browns have been good at stopping the run for the better part of the past two decades.

According to numbers pulled by Chris Easterling at The Beacon Journal, the Browns are currently ranked No. 24 against the run as they are allowing 126.9 yards per game. Only once since 1999 have the Browns allowed less than 100 yards per game in a season, and that came in the winless campaign of 2017.

Even under the great and mighty Schwartz, the Browns struggled, as in his three seasons the defense allowed 105.5 rushing yards per game (2023), 129.7 in 2024, and 116.4 in 2025.

It doesn't seem as if the offense is in any hurry to put a full game together, so the defense is going to have to tighten up against the run if there is any hope of not having the season spiral away.

This week will be a good test to see if the coaches can make any meaningful changes as the Browns face a New Orleans team that is No. 28 in rushing yards (86.0), No. 30 in yards per carry (3.52), and just fired its offensive run coordinator.

If the Browns can't keep the Saints under control on the ground, there is no telling how bad things may get the rest of the way.

#2804. Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac rally as Ackman presses for conservatorship exit

The midterm elections could be a turning point for the release of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac from government control, according to billionaire investor Bill Ackman.

Investors may agree with him, if the rally in both stocks is any sign.

The Federal National Mortgage Association, known as Fannie Mae, and Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corporation, or Freddie Mac, have each jumped more than 60% from Oct. 14 to Monday's close. The stocks were both up roughly 3% on Tuesday.

Ackman, the founder of Pershing Square Capital Management, has long pushed for the two entities to be released from federal conservatorship.

"The reason why it's not being touched right now is, you know, midterms," he said in an interview with CNBC's "Squawk Box."

Ackman, who owns both names through Pershing Square, believes Freddie and Fannie have the potential to increase "10-fold from current share prices," he said in his quarterly letter to shareholders, issued on Monday.

Fannie and Freddie buy mortgages from banks and other lenders, and then package them into mortgage-backed securities, known as MBS. Their operations are critical to the housing market, providing liquidity to banks and creating a secondary market for MBS.

The entities were placed into conservatorship in September 2008, during the financial crisis. The stocks were delisted from the New York Stock Exchange in 2010 and have traded over the counter since then.

Ackman wants the conservatorship to end, arguing the entities would be worth multiples of their current valuation if they were freed from government control.

President Donald Trump has supported ending the conservatorship of Fannie and Freddie. But it remains politically and economically contentious.

The entities operate under strict capital threshold requirements and would need to be recapitalized, which could happen through issuing common equity. However, the Treasury Department would need to figure out an exit plan for its roughly $388 billion ownership stake in the entities through preferred securities and warrants.

Congress may also need to play a role, passing legislation to restructure the government's role in mortgage financing and home-loan guarantees.

Nonetheless, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent recently said it could happen before Trump's term ends, telling 2Way's "The Morning Meeting" podcast that the administration will tackle the ownership structure "next year, the year after." He said affordability will be guiding the decision.

One point of controversy is whether ending the conservatorship of Fannie and Freddie would increase the spreads on MBS over Treasuries, effectively making mortgages costlier. Bessent has sought to reassure the market that wouldn't happen.

"Whatever we do is going to be guided by making sure that the spread on [agency] mortgages … over the Treasury does not increase," Bessent said.

Ackman argues that privatizing the GSEs would help insulate them from political meddling. "Fannie and Freddie are these massive, enormously profitable institutions where whichever political party controls them…if they're still in conservatorship, can influence the outcome of elections," he told CNBC.

In one scenario, he explained, Democrats win the White House, conservatorship is still in place, and Democrats push Fannie and Freddie to lower credit standards in order to expand home ownership and affordability.

"If they're going to move more aggressively into borrowers with lower credit quality, for example, to achieve a political objective, that's going to have an impact on trillions of dollars outstanding mortgage securities," Ackman said. "It's going to have an impact on overall credit spreads."

MBS investors want certainty about how the entities will be run, he noted.

"That only gets resolved in a world in which they exit conservatorship, they become publicly traded companies that are owned by institutional and retail investors," Ackman said. "We set the rules. In conservatorship, the president can do anything."

#2801. Dumont family takes controlling ownership of Mavericks after purchasing shares from Miriam Adelson

Sivan and Patrick Dumont are now the controlling owners of the Dallas Mavericks.

The Dumonts purchased Miriam Adelson's shares of the Mavericks last month, according to ESPN's Tim MacMahon, which made them the controlling owners of the team with a 69% ownership share.

Though she has sold her shares to the Dumonts, Adelson is still very much connected to the Mavericks. Patrick Dumont, who has served as the Mavericks' governor since the families purchased the team from Mark Cuban in 2023, is Adelson's son-in-law. Sivan is Adelson's daughter.

"It's really about long-term investment in the city of Dallas," Dumont told ESPN on Tuesday. "The Dumont family is really committed to building what we hope is the best arena in the NBA, a really significant investment in the city that will help create the new 40-year home for the Dallas Mavericks, a great experience for our fans and inspire our team to win championships. That's really what we're focused on. We had the opportunity, and we're really excited about it."

Cuban sold the Mavericks to Adelson at a $3.5 billion valuation in 2023, though he still maintains a 27% share of the team. He's since admitted that he regretted selling the Mavericks to Adelson and Dumont in the first place, especially after the Dumonts and Adelson pushed him out of the team's basketball and business operations side. Cuban's comments came in the wake of the Luka Doncic trade, which drew intense backlash from Mavericks fans and resulted in an overhaul of the team.

Dumont, who is the Las Vegas Sands CEO, can purchase another 20% share of the team from Cuban in the future at the same valuation, too, something he said he plans to do.

"I just have to tell you, I love Mark. He's been a great family friend for a really long time," Dumont said. "He's just a super passionate Mavs fan and he's frustrated. I respect it. We're going to hopefully do him proud. That's my goal — to make all of our Mavs fans super proud about the success of the team and win a championship."

The Mavericks are expected to open a new arena at the Valley View Mall site in north Dallas in the coming years, and hope to have a new business office and practice facility to go with it. Dumont has overseen construction of the Venetian Arena in Macao, which is home to the NBA's preseason games in the country.

The Mavericks have played at the American Airlines Center since 2001, and hope to move into the new arena in time for the 2031-32 campaign.

"I think what we bring to Dallas is going to be world class," Dumont said. "My goal is to make the best arena in the NBA. It starts with the court and expands outwards, and I want to make sure the fans have the best experience possible, because we owe it to them."

The Mavericks currently hold a 4-3 record entering a matchup with the San Antonio Spurs on Wednesday night. They've not been to the playoffs since their trip to the NBA Finals with Doncic in 2024, and went just 26-56 last season.

#2798. Binance breach puts custody at center of crypto infrastructure trade

The $6.3 billion Binance hack could accelerate a shift in how investors value cryptocurrency companies, putting a greater premium on custody providers and the infrastructure needed to securely hold and protect digital assets.

Much of crypto's evolution this year has involved companies moving past their reliance on trading volumes and transaction fees, to focus instead on building the infrastructure connecting digital assets with traditional finance. Last Thursday's breach adds a new dimension, bringing cybersecurity, custody, compliance and balance-sheet resilience into sharper focus.

Importantly, the Binance breach was not an indictment of crypto itself, or a case of leadership-driven fraud, as with FTX in late 2022. Instead, Binance's leadership moved quickly to contain the fallout, protect customers and commit the exchange's own resources to cover losses.

On Tuesday, Binance CEO Richard Teng told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" that the company has replenished 98% of $6.34 billion in affected assets, and that it is still in the process of purchasing outstanding, more illiquid assets.

Management's response, alongside efforts elsewhere in the industry to boost confidence, helped prevent a security breach from escalating into a broader crisis of confidence. For example, Tether, Circle, Ripple and others moved quickly to freeze or restrict access to about $3 billion in stolen assets; Coinbase blocked transfers to compromised wallets and offered Binance direct assistance.

The hack could even help shape the next phase of the crypto infrastructure trade. The new winners may not just be the businesses with the most users, volume or assets under custody, but the ones that can also demonstrate they're able to protect those assets under extreme duress.

"Which company has the resources to invest in cybersecurity and protect customer funds? For a smaller company, it could be much harder because once these crypto companies become infrastructure plays, providing the well for tokenization … they need to have the compliance and control in place so that a similar hacking will not happen or can be minimized," Owen Lau, senior analyst at ClearStreet, told CNBC. "Larger companies have more resources that could give them some advantage."

While institutional investors have increasingly embraced digital assets, broader adoption depends on confidence that those assets can be securely held, accessed and transferred. The Binance breach highlights the importance of that infrastructure, and could increase demand for specialized custodians and platforms with established asset-protection capabilities.

Coinbase has operated a dedicated institutional custody business since 2018. Circle entered the custody business this year, after the U.S. Office of the Comptroller of the Currency granted it approval to operate as a trust bank. In the past few years, Ripple and Kraken have also launched custody businesses.

Still, smaller players compete in the space as well. Small cap crypto exchange stock Gemini Space Station has offered custody services since 2019. BitGo Holdings, founded in 2013, is one of the earliest players in institutional crypto custody and infrastructure, with a reputation for security and serving major institutions.

The shift could also drive consolidation as companies look to buy capabilities, deepen their infrastructure offerings and achieve the scale needed to compete, Lau said.

The more consequential structural shift may be the separation of custody from execution, according to Morgan Stanley.

"Crypto exchanges have historically combined trading, custody, and settlement within vertically integrated platforms, concentrating operational risk. Repeated security breaches could encourage investors to move assets toward independent custody while continuing to trade on CEXs," the firm's analyst Felix Stratmann said in a note Monday," referring to centralized cryptocurrency exchanges.

"This would preserve the role of centralized exchanges as liquidity and execution venues, while potentially benefiting regulated custodians, including banks, as institutional investors place greater emphasis on asset segregation, operational resilience, and investor protection," Stratmann said.

#2793. Penn State’s successful ground game against Purdue stems from bye week

Three weeks ago, Penn State football coach Matt Campbell and offensive coordinator Taylor Mouser sounded frustrated with the offense in general and the running game in particular.

The Nittany Lions' struggles continued the following week against Michigan before their bye week. The coaches spent the next two weeks pushing the offensive line to be more physical and searching to find the right combination at running back.

After averaging 75 rushing yards in its first four Big Ten games, Penn State ran for 269 in its 31-17 victory over Purdue last weekend.

"I would say I was desperate," Mouser said Tuesday. "When you're not winning here and you're not living up to the standard, you feel like you're letting a lot more people down than just the players and the coaches.

"For those guys to go out there and play with that level of physicality, violence and conviction, to be able to see real chemistry and real communication at the line, we looked like a real football team at times in the game."

It was the second-highest rushing total by Penn State this season, falling short of the 304 yards it had against Buffalo. It also was just the fourth time in the last 15 games against an opponent from a Power Four conference that a Campbell-coached team scored at least 30 points.

Cam Wallace, who was in effect the fourth-team running back, impressed Campbell and Mouser in practice the last two weeks to earn his first career start. He rushed 22 times for 135 yards, both career highs, after getting just 22 carries in the first seven games.

"What you guys saw Saturday was what we saw on the practice field the last two weeks," Campbell said about Wallace. "It was cut and dried. It was easy. When it's not cut and dried, it's really hard to make tough decisions when everybody's competing.

"When you leave it gray, we can make mistakes. When you don't leave it gray, you leave yourself in a great situation and then you capitalize on it."

Besides Wallace, Carson Hansen ran 17 times for a season-high 96 yards and a touchdown.

"I'm really proud of Cam and Carson and the way those guys ran," Mouser said. "We really challenged the whole running back room. To be able to have somebody draw a line in the sand and say, 'I'm going to be the guy,' those guys did a great job during the bye week and left no doubt.

"When it wasn't perfect, Cam was running at the level that our running backs have to play at from a physicality, attitude and effort standpoint."

Penn State's offensive line played its best game of the season, perhaps not coincidentally against a defense that ranked 97th or worse nationally in every major category. Its performance came after the coaches concentrated on improving the linemen's physicality.

The last two weeks, they worked on blocking double teams in the running game for 20-minute clips during the period usually set aside for individual drills.

"I wanted them to buy more into the mentality of what it takes to run the ball," Mouser said. "It doesn't necessarily matter what the calls are. Those guys have to be excited and sprint to the line of scrimmage. It's going to be physical. It's going to be violent. It's going to be downhill.

"We had really, really physical bye week practices. It wasn't an off week for our guys. I was probably more proud that we had the ball for 43 minutes than anything else."

Penn State (1-4 Big Ten, 4-4) will face a stronger defense when it meets Washington (2-3, 5-3) Saturday at 3:30 (TV-FS1) in Seattle. The Huskies rank 42nd in scoring defense and 54th in total defense and rushing defense.

Campbell hopes that simplifying the offense during the bye week will help the Lions have success again this week.

"Sometimes as coaches – and I'm at fault for this as much as anybody – you're trying to over-scheme to put yourself in the best position at the moment," he said. "When you can sit down and digest it all, you say, 'OK, this is what we're best at. Let's make sure we're teaching what we can do best.'

"That really has been the emphasis since the USC game. We had a little more time to attack it during the bye week. We were able to find a little bit better rhythm in terms of how we want to run the football."

#2789. Bengals Film Room: Chase Brown starting to heat up?

The Cincinnati Bengals survived an overtime thriller 43-36 on Sunday against the Tennessee Titans. No one expected the game to be that close, but that is life in the NFL. If you start out slow, you are typically in for a dogfight the rest of the day. That is something that the Bengals continue to keep doing.

There has been a lot of chatter about trading for a running back, specifically Jonathan Taylor. While Taylor is a great back, I have not been of the belief that he necessarily elevates this team dramatically. For a guy that would cost premium draft capital to acquire, he would be joining a Bengals team that will always be pass-first.

When you pass the ball a lot, you need a player that is a high-level pass protector and can catch the ball out of the backfield. To me, they already have that guy in Chase Brown.

Brown caught eight passes for 46 yards on Sunday. He had a fantastic touchdown reception, but it was called back due to a holding call on Dylan Fairchild. Brown is a reliable target as a pass catcher, and that is something the Bengals will need to continue leaning on as an extension of the running game this season.

The thing that Brown has improved the most on since his time in the NFL is his pass protection. He has turned himself into one of the best pass protectors in the league this season. He has a 78.2 pass-blocking grade and has consistently flashed by picking up blitzes all season. For a team that loves to throw the ball, it's so critical to have guys like Brown and Perine who take pride in being good blockers for Joe Burrow and the offense.

While it wasn't a massively productive rushing performance for Brown on Sunday, it felt efficient. Brown had 12 carries for 55 rushing yards. That totals out to 4.6 yards per carry in the game. I thought he has looked more elusive, quick to hit the hole, and has been running his best of the season over the last two weeks.

If Chase Brown is the running back #1 for the rest of the season, you have to hope that this is the start of him coming on for the rest of the season. He has been a player who has started a bit slower statistically in the past. Just last season, he did not have a rushing game over 50 yards until Week 7. He still finished the season with over 1,000 rushing yards.

If the Bengals want to compete in the playoffs, they'll need more balance in the running game. Chase Brown starting to heat up would go a long way toward accomplishing that.

#2785. Kyler Murray's hamstring issue could be cover for a soft benching

How can the Vikings bench Kyler Murray without benching Kyler Murray?

They can rely on an injury through which he otherwise would be able to play.

It’s hard not to look at the current status of Murray’s hamstring “tightness” as cover for a soft benching of Murray. That gives the Vikings a chance to let Carson Wentz, who played well enough in most of the Week 1 win over the Packers and all of the Week 2 win over the Bears.

While the Vikings will never admit to that strategy, consider this undeniable fact: On Tuesday, offensive coordinator Wes Phillips was asked for an assessment of Murray’s play “in the past couple weeks.”

“I don’t really want to get into, like, overarching, ‘Hey, this is this is the . . .,” Phillips said. “You know, the fact of the matter is, you know, we lost the game against a tough [Lions] football team on the road. It’s a division game. It stings, but we’ve got to get better moving forward.  And, you know, we’ll see as the week goes on, where we’re at in that spot . . . but, yeah, we’ve got to get better. We’re going to actively pursue every avenue we can to make that happen.”

This implies, if taken literally, pursuing every avenue toward acquiring an upgrade via a trade — whether that’s Jacoby Brissett, Daniel Jones, Kirk Cousins, or even Justin Herbert.

It all comes down to whether the Vikings are content to keep doing what they’ve been doing, or whether they’ll make a move aimed at significantly upgrading a position that, in recent weeks, has not been good enough.

Yes, they’re 6-1. That’s better than anyone could have expected them to be. But it’s not because Murray has turned the clock back to the early years of his career. His passer rating (86.6) is toward the bottom of all qualifying quarterbacks (and, in fairness, that’s higher than the numbers generated by Brissett, Jones, and Herbert).

It’s the lowest number for any season of Murray’s career, and the overall performance is less than what the Vikings need to maximize their current formula.

Especially since he’s not getting the ball to receiver Justin Jefferson. That’s something Wentz did consistently in 2025, making Wentz the preferred option to J.J. McCarthy — who returned to the lineup following a Week 2 ankle injury only after Wentz suffered a season-ending shoulder injury in Week 8.

If McCarthy was still in Minnesota, there would be an unavoidable groundswell to give him a shot. But he lost the No. 2 job to Wentz. Which means Wentz won it.

Which means that the Vikings could be thinking about giving Wentz a Monday night audition against the Bills, with a plan to make a possible trade the next day if things don’t go well.

For now, the rest of the week will reveal whether and to what extent Murray or Wentz will take the first-team reps at practice. And whether Murray or Wentz will play on Monday night.

It won’t be a surprise if it’s Wentz against the Bills. Even if Murray is technically healthy enough to play.

Bama started slowly and led only 6-2 with 15:52 left in the half. With 14:55 remains the Tide led 6-5 and were 0-7 from three point range. Oats was liberally substituting, bringing guys in by pairs every couple of minutes. With under 14 minutes on the clock Jemison finally hit the teams first long range shot for an 11-7 lead. Highly regarded freshman Jaxon Richardson had a highlight reel dunk on a breakaway to follow up for at 13-7 lead.

Freshman point guard Anderson Diaz got his first action of the year, bouncing back from a wrist injury that had kept him sidelined. With 10:08 left the Tide was on pace for 56 points, holding a lead of 14-10. Tarris Bouie followed an Allen hoop with a fantastic windmill dunk for a lead of 20-12 with 8:10 remaining.

Fielder and Bouie both hit from long range, followed by another pair from Jemison for a 37-20 lead at the 3:45 mark. The Bearkats shrunk the margin to 40-29 at the break. Oats used eight players at least 10 minutes or more in the period.

The Tide shot 16-38 for 42% in the half, with only 4-15 for 27% from deep, while making 4-6 free throws. Bama had 24 rebounds, with eight on the offensive end, with eight assists, seven blocks, 7 steals, and committed seven turnovers.

Sam Houston made 9-30 shots for 30%, including 5-15 for 33% from deep. SH was 6-10 at the line, grabbed 22 rebounds, had four assists, three blocks, six steals, and gave the ball away 11 times. Coleman scored 10 points and Pipkin added eight to lead the team.

Alabama used the same starting lineup in the second half and quickly put the game away. The Tide scored in the paint out of the break and with 18:55 left Jemison nailed another long range jumper for a 45-29 lead. When the margin reached 18 at 49-31, Sam Houston called a timeout. After the timeout Samuels hit from long distance and the lead was 21. Bama's length and aggressiveness on defense was bothering the Bearkats as the lead ballooned. Keitenn Bristow hit a three pointer for a 61-34 lead with 14:34 left in the game. Oats continued to rotate guys in and out, and everyone was contributing. With 3:50 left the lead swole to 90-61. Oats was upset after the game when Sam Houston outscored the Tide 13-6 over the remainder of the game.

In the second half Alabama was 20-37 for 54% in the period with 6-16 for 38% from deep and 14-19 at the charity stripe. Overall the Tide finished 36-75 for 48%, 10-31 for 32 % from three, and 14-19 for 74% at the line. Bama finished with 42 rebounds,- 13 offensively-, 17 assists, 10 blocks, 17 steals, and 10 turnovers. Fiedler tied for the team lead with 15 points and had six rebounds and one assist. Jemison also had 15 on 6-7 shooting including 3-4 from three point range, and added three rebounds, two steals, and an assist. Bouie continued to impress with 13 points, seven rebounds, two assist, two steals, and a block. Allen scored 12 points, grabbed four rebounds, dished out four assists, had two steals and blocked a shot while not committing any turnovers as the primary ball handler. Garrison won the hard hat with nine points, four rebounds, two blocks, three steals, and seven deflections. Samuels also had nine points to go with a team leading five assists and four steals. Bristow has the look of the ultimate garbage man for the Tide, scoring five points with three rebounds, four blocks and two steals. Sharp shooting freshman guard Cole Cloer had a tough opener, going 1-9 from the field including 0-6 from three point land.

Sam Houston shot 16-35 for 46% in the second stanza with 10-18 for 56% from deep and 3-6 at the free throw line. Overall the Kats were 25-65 for 39%, with 15-33 for 46% from three, and 9-16 for 56% at the line. Sam Houston finished with 45 rebounds, 15 offensively, 17 assists, six blocks, seven steals, and 23 turnovers. Coleman was the leading scored with 16 points with six rebounds and an assist. Begg added 13 points, four rebounds, and four assists. St. Bernard had five points and was the games leading rebounder with eight and tossed in three assists.

Next up is another home game at Friday at 6:30 p.m. CT on Friday. The Tide will host Arkansas State, and can be seen on SEC Network Plus.

#2771. When the game is on the line, where has Devin Booker gone?

There was an unfortunate trend that began to manifest itself during the back half of last season. When the going gets tough, your best players need to get going. And unfortunately for the Phoenix Suns, that trend involved Devin Booker's struggles to perform in clutch moments.

From February 1 onward, in 11 clutch games in which Booker played, the Suns went 3-8. During those moments, Booker shot 6-of-20 from the field, recorded five assists against eight turnovers, and posted a -34 plus/minus.

That's concerning, especially when you consider that over his previous 10 seasons, which included some pretty horrible Suns teams, Booker owned a -2 +/- in 316 clutch situations. He shot 40% from the field during those moments and maintained a 1.8 assist-to-turnover ratio.

And it wasn't as if Booker had struggled in the clutch throughout the entirety of last season. Through the first 19 games in which he played, the Suns were 11-8 in clutch situations. Booker shot 51.2% from the field, recorded 10 assists against only three turnovers, and posted a +27 plus/minus. But upon returning from an ankle injury on February 7, the nosedive began.

You can make the argument that it's supposed to be tough, that your best player is naturally going to be the focal point of opposing defenses, and therefore his performance will be hindered by the schemes designed to stop him. During that same timeframe, from February 1 onward, Booker ranked dead last in plus/minus among players who attempted at least 20 shots in clutch situations. Jalen Brunson, Luka Doncic, and Shai Gilgeous-Alexander were at the top of the list, with Brunson posting a +41. And there were plenty of other names ahead of Booker, including Jamal Murray, CJ McCollum, Brandon Ingram, and Desmond Bane.

That only adds to the concern about who Devin Booker is and what he represents at this point in his career, particularly within the context of this Suns team. Because you can make excuses all day long about how he's being double-teamed or triple-teamed, but great players make the necessary adjustments that lead to team success. That's why plus/minus, when evaluated over an extended period, carries considerably more value than looking at the number from a single game. The trend we witnessed last season was concerning.

If double teams are being thrown at Devin Booker, why is he turning the ball over so frequently? Does he not see them coming? You know as well as I do that many of those turnovers come from Booker predictably driving into a crowd of defenders and trying to force the issue rather than relying on the finesse that's been a hallmark of his career.

Why do I bring this up? Because on Monday night against the Golden State Warriors, that familiar trend once again manifested itself. Booker's inability to execute in clutch moments ultimately contributed to another Suns loss. Yes, there are multiple variables involved, including other players who failed to perform when it mattered most. But none of those guys are making $57 million a year.

Booker re-entered the game with the Suns leading 106-104 and 4:48 remaining. A minute later, he connected on a nine-foot jumper, accounting for his only two points in clutch time. From there, things unraveled.

With Phoenix trailing 109-108, Booker missed a wide-open 12-foot jumper. On the following possession, he turned the ball over. After Jalen Green committed a turnover on the next trip down the floor, Booker was called for an offensive foul, his sixth and final foul of the game.

His final clutch stat line? In 3.8 minutes, Booker shot 1-of-2 from the field, grabbed one rebound, committed two turnovers, and posted a -7 plus/minus.

It's not the end of the world, but it does raise concerns that Devin Booker is picking up right where he left off last season, when his ability to impose his will on a game appeared to be a fading trait.

You might look at this as a one-game sample, but I see it as a sample of 11 previous clutch-time games. Perhaps that's still not enough to definitively identify a trend, especially when you consider the body of work Booker has put together over what is now his 12th NBA season. But it's the manner in which these struggles recur, time and again, that has become the focal point of frustration for a fan base desperate for success and watching a team that can ill afford to lose.

Booker's game has become predictable, and his execution in these moments has been subpar. And I know that somewhere, somebody is preparing to show me a collection of all the game winners Booker has made throughout his career. I appreciate every one of those moments and what they've meant to us as Suns fans. In the same breath, hitting a game-winner against Oklahoma City last season doesn't equate to a victory last night against Golden State.

Devin Booker has earned the benefit of the doubt throughout his career, but that doesn't mean he's exempt from scrutiny when the results begin telling a different story. The Suns need their best player to be their best player when possessions matter most. That requires better decisions, cleaner execution, and an ability to recognize what opposing defenses are taking away. Booker's past has established what he's capable of. His present is beginning to raise legitimate questions about his ability to consistently deliver it.

#2769. How Brian Schottenheimer is failing the Cowboys

Watching the Dallas Cowboys in 2026 has become a tiring experience. We are not even halfway through the season, and things are already looking bleak. Losing is never fun, but watching them underachieve has become a weekly ordeal that has turned into pure exhaustion.

Every Sunday, it's a new level of disappointment. There's talent on this team, but the leadership and tactical execution have brought about regular failures that are tough to sit through. The most recent collapse against the Arizona Cardinals serves as more evidence that head coach and play-caller Brian Schottenheimer is fundamentally not the guy to help this franchise return to glory.

The issues start with Schottenheimer's bizarre tendencies. He routinely fails to make the basic decisions that would maximize his team's probability of winning. One example is his weird habit of running quarterback sneaks down at his own goal line. Instead of trusting his playmakers or scheming an effective play, he plays scared and chooses to waste a down, putting the offense in a tough spot. Every time he does this, the Cowboys have punted three plays later.

Another example is his treatment of Brandon Aubrey. We all know that Aubrey is one of the league's most lethal kicking weapons, but Schottenheimer finds ways to turn that into a disadvantage for the Cowboys.

Rather than pressing and trying to pick up extra yards to give him a more reasonable field goal attempt, the head coach contentedly runs the ball and settles for a short gain. His confidence in Aubrey treats those situations like an automatic three points instead of working for a shorter attempt. He unnecessarily creates high-stress kicking situations that have resulted in blocks and misses.

The team also cannot stop repeating the same mistakes. They look uncoached at times, committing the same self-inflicted errors week after week. Are we sick of neutral zone infractions yet? Every week. Early and often. It's just the same penalties over and over. It's become an epidemic. Whatever the coaches are doing to discourage this practice is not working. They keep jumping early.

As a play-caller, Schottenheimer is equally frustrating. The team doesn't have much of a rushing attack, as the offense has struggled to deploy the physical ground game they so confidently promote during the summer. It's been ineffective, and there have been moments when he has completely abandoned it, essentially acknowledging defeat.

That admission might be a little easier to accept if the offense possessed a high-powered aerial attack that many believe should accompany having one of the best wide receiving duos in the league. But they don't.

For some reason, the team's most explosive receiving weapons are underutilized. Schottenheimer fails to create mismatches, and the offense becomes very stagnant at times. No pre-snap motion or creative blocking schemes. The Cowboys' offense has turned into a predictable entity that defenses can absolutely shut down at certain points in the game, and those moments are extremely harmful.

Under Schottenheimer, the Cowboys constantly invent new ways to lose football games. Against the Cardinals, it was the inability to run out the clock. Earlier in the year, against the Ravens, it was a goal-line debauchery that couldn't win the game. Both instances put the pressure back on a porous defense to come through, and sadly, they did not.

The Cowboys don't just lose. They actively engineer their own downfall through a blend of situational ineptitude and executive panic.

But if you listen to Schottenheimer's postgame press conferences, he seems completely detached from reality. His media appearances have turned into comedy shows, highlighted by delusion and a lack of awareness. He stands at the table and claims to be a problem solver, yet no problems ever get solved. He throws out tired clichés and empty promises about how things need to get cleaned up, but each week the same chaos ensues.

The Cowboys are a 3-5 football team, and sadly, it's fitting for who they are. Each week, they are favored against these bad teams because, on paper, they should be beating them. They have more talent. But none of that matters when the coaching puts them at such a disadvantage.

Star players become average, and average players become bad. So far, the evidence strongly suggests that Schottenheimer is not a head coach capable of leading an NFL team to victory, and with each new week, this is becoming more and more obvious.

#2766. Raptors storm back to stun Clippers in fourth-quarter comeback

INGLEWOOD, CALIFORNIA – NOVEMBER 02: Baba Miller #18 of the LA Clippers defends against the dribble of Scottie Barnes #4 of the Toronto Raptors during the first half of a game at Intuit Dome on November 02, 2026 in Inglewood, California.NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. (Photo by Sean M. Haffey/Getty Images) | Getty Images

The Toronto Raptors completed a double-digit comeback to defeat the Los Angeles Clippers 125-118 at the Intuit Dome.

Toronto, which did not take its first lead until the final two minutes, came through with a clutch fourth-quarter rally to secure the win.

The Raptors found themselves in a similar position against the Lakers the previous night, but their comeback attempt fell short. This time, however, Toronto learned from that experience and finished the job with a hard-fought victory.

The Raptors continued to experiment with their options at centre, giving Trayce Jackson-Davis an opportunity last night before turning to Collin Murray-Boyles tonight, as Jakob Poeltl did not play.

Both teams traded possessions early, with neither side looking particularly sharp offensively. Trading baskets remained the theme for much of the opening quarter, as both teams struggled to find a consistent rhythm.

However, the Clippers began to create some separation behind their three-point shooting. Kobe Sanders led the charge late in the frame, scoring 11 points on 4-of-6 shooting, including 3-of-4 from beyond the arc as the Raptors had no answer for him.

Los Angeles closed the quarter on a 17-5 run, extending its lead to as many as 13 points before heading into the second quarter with an 11-point advantage.

Toronto looked sloppy down the stretch and simply didn't do enough to start the game.

The Raptors showed some signs of life to start the second quarter, with Immanuel Quickley getting Toronto on the board before Scottie Barnes added his first basket of the night. Barnes, who entered the game questionable, had been relatively quiet through the opening stretch.

RJ Barrett also provided a spark offensively, knocking down a three-pointer before scoring on a post-up jumper against former teammate Gradey Dick to bring his total to 16 points.

Toronto's three-point shooting and defensive effort improved, but the Clippers continued to respond whenever the Raptors threatened to build momentum.

Brook Lopez continued to give Toronto problems, taking advantage of the Raptors' smaller lineup on both ends of the floor.

Turnovers also became a major issue for Toronto, with seven giveaways leading to nine Clippers points. Dick continued to put together a strong performance as Los Angeles extended its lead to as many as 15 points.

Toronto also had to manage much of the quarter without Barrett, who picked up his third personal foul. The Raptors had plenty of work to do after heading into halftime trailing 63-52.

INGLEWOOD, CA – NOVEMBER 2: RJ Barrett #9 of the Toronto Raptors looks to pass the ball as Max Strus #31 of the LA Clippers plays defense during the game on November 2, 2026 at Intuit Dome in Los Angeles, California. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and/or using this Photograph, user is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. Mandatory Copyright Notice: Copyright 2026 NBAE (Photo by Juan Ocampo/NBAE via Getty Images) | NBAE via Getty Images

Toronto came out of the halftime break with much better energy, as Barnes, Walter and Murray-Boyles helped spark a 6-0 run to cut the Clippers' lead to five. The strong start forced Los Angeles to call an early timeout, but the Clippers quickly settled back into the game and restored their nine-point advantage.

Dick and Sanders continued to build on their impressive nights, with Dick making an impact across the floor and Sanders knocking down a three-pointer to cap an 11-3 Clippers run.

Toronto continued to struggle offensively, with Barrett providing a strong performance but receiving very little help from the rest of the lineup.

Jamison Battle provided a much-needed spark off the bench, knocking down back-to-back three-pointers to bring his total to 12 points. Battle was particularly effective from beyond the arc, shooting 4-of-5 from three-point range.

Although Toronto showed some improvement towards the end of the quarter, the Clippers maintained control and carried a 13-point lead into the fourth. The Raptors needed a strong final quarter, similar to last night if they wanted to make a comeback.

Toronto opened the fourth quarter with back-to-back baskets from Alijah Martin and Scottie Barnes, who quietly recorded a double-double. Barnes and RJ Barrett began to find a rhythm together offensively, helping Toronto chip away at the deficit, while Immanuel Quickley added a pull-up three-pointer to cut the lead to eight.

However, foul trouble continued to be an issue for the Raptors, with Ja'Kobe Walter picking up his fifth personal foul and Barrett his fourth, allowing the Clippers to extend their advantage back to 12.

Los Angeles also lost Brook Lopez to fouls, as he fouled out with five minutes remaining, giving Toronto a potential opening to make a push.

With both teams showing signs of fatigue, Toronto continued to battle and took advantage of opportunities at the free-throw line to work its way back into the game.

Barnes, Quickley and Barrett had carried much of the offensive load throughout the night, and they delivered when it mattered most. Barrett converted a tough layup with under three minutes remaining to tie the game at 109, capping a remarkable 16-4 Raptors run.

Barnes followed with a difficult turnaround fadeaway to give Toronto its first lead of the night. Some clutch free throws from Barnes, Murray-Boyles and Quickley, combined with vintage defensive intensity down the stretch, helped the Raptors complete the fourth-quarter comeback and escape Los Angeles with a hard-fought victory.

Although it was far from a perfect performance, the Raptors showed resilience and refused to give up, earning a crucial victory.

Barnes, Quickley and Barrett led the way for Toronto with strong performances. However, there is still room for improvement, particularly with their three-point shooting, free-throw efficiency and ability to get off to a stronger start.

Raptors fans were hoping to see Kawhi Leonard face his former team, but neither Leonard nor Brandon Ingram suited up. Dick, however, delivered a solid performance against his former team, while Sanders led the Clippers with 26 points. Despite his efforts, Los Angeles could not hold on to its lead and fell to 1-6 on the season.

"This achievement is incredibly inspiring. The coaching staff gave their all to help the players perform. It's an undeniable achievement, because it's our first national youth league title. The São Paulo side's head coach, Guilherme Nascimento, explained that the title was the result of a process of connecting the players with the club's "spirit and history."

#2757. Penn State notes: WR Chase Sowell is on track to play at Washington

Penn State probably will have at least one injured wide receiver on the trip later this week to Washington, coach Matt Campbell said Tuesday.

Chase Sowell, the Nittany Lions' leading receiver, missed last week's 31-17 win over Purdue with a leg injury. Koby Howard, who averaged almost 29 yards a catch in the first three games, has missed the last five games, also with a leg injury.

"The word 'probable' is what I would use with Chase," Campbell said. "I think he's in a really good spot. I think Koby is still probably in the word 'questionable,' and I think we'll have to see where he's at.

"It's the same rhetoric that I guess I've said the last couple weeks. When he's ready, we're going to try to make sure he's on the field, but we're going to make sure he's ready to go."

Sowell, a senior, has 34 receptions for 510 yards and three touchdowns. A sophomore, Howard has 12 catches for 344 yards and two TDs.

Without Sowell and Howard, Penn State tight ends Andrew Rappleyea, Ben Brahmer and Gabe Burkle combined for nine catches for 115 yards and one TD against Purdue.

"You have to find a way to create explosive plays," offensive coordinator Taylor Mouser said. "When you don't have some of your most explosive athletes, it makes things hard. We always cater to the personnel that we have, whether it's the running backs, the tight ends or the other wide receivers."

Penn State cornerback Audavion Collins picked up the first carry of his career when he rushed for 11 yards in the fourth quarter against Purdue.

"We didn't have a ton of guys who could be like AC," Mouser said. "I've been thinking about it for a long time. …He's one of the faster guys that we have. It was good to see him go out there and create an explosive play for us."

Collins is in his second season as a starter for the Lions after he transferred from Mississippi State following the 2022 season. He leads Penn State with nine pass breakups.

"I just love what that kid's about," Mouser said. "He just loves football. He's tenacious."

Penn State backup quarterback Alex Manske hasn't taken a snap in Big Ten play and probably won't the rest of the year unless one of the four remaining games gets out of hand one way or the other.

Campbell was asked Tuesday whether he will try to get him snaps to prepare for next season when starter Rocco Becht's eligibility will have expired.

"It's a really fair question," Campbell said. "When the lights come on and you get the opportunity to play, what does it look like? Whether we get those opportunities to foster that, that'll be great. That is not my intent.

"My intent is to have this team playing its best football down the stretch, and that continues to be our priority. But if those opportunities would ever exist, we're going to do everything in our power to try to get Alex in the football game."

Penn State's traveling party for the Washington game Saturday at 3:30 p.m. (TV-FS1) will ride on buses Thursday from State College to Harrisburg International Airport, where it will take a direct flight to Seattle.

The last two years, the Lions also traveled on Thursday to Los Angeles for games against USC in 2024 and UCLA in 2025.

"The time of the game was really big," Campbell said when asked why they're leaving Thursday. "I guess it's a 12:35 start time there. I felt like if we got in Friday, boy, you're going to be really pushing it.

"In our past (at Iowa State), we've had to go to the West Coast. If it was a day game, we tried to go on Thursday to get ourselves there, get settled in and try to, from a sleep standpoint, get on the best rhythm that we possibly can and not lose sleep."

#2756. Bo Nix has 15 game-winning drives, most ever for a QB in his first three seasons

The Broncos trailed the Chiefs 24-13 with 10 minutes left on Sunday, but anyone who thought the Broncos were out of it hasn’t been watching Bo Nix.

Nix led Denver’s offense to two touchdowns and a two-point conversion in the fourth quarter of a 28-24 win, marking Nix’s 15th career game-winning drive in the fourth quarter or overtime. No quarterback in NFL history has as many game-winning drives in his first three seasons as Nix.

Dak Prescott, who had 14 game-winning drives in his first three seasons, had the previous record. Nix has surpassed Prescott and isn’t even halfway through his third season.

A game-winning drive is defined as an offensive scoring drive in the fourth quarter or overtime that puts a team ahead for the final time. Nix had three of them as a rookie in 2024, an NFL-high seven of them last year, and has an NFL-high five of them already this year.

The all-time leader in game-winning drives is Tom Brady, who had 58 of them. It would take Nix many years to catch Brady, but being more than a quarter of the way there through two and a half seasons is an impressive achievement.

#2741. The troubling Nets trend holding them back for yet another year

Jordi Fernández sat inside the visitors news conference room at Madison Square Garden and looked at the paper boxscore in front of him following the Nets' 103-90 loss Monday to the reigning champs.

"I mean, you hold a team to 103 points in the NBA, you should be able to win a lot of games," Fernández said.

Even if tanking is in Brooklyn's rearview mirror, its offense remains stuck in the past.

In Fernández's first season, Cam Thomas — who is no longer in the NBA — was the leading scorer on a 26-win team that ranked 28th in scoring (105.1) and offensive rating. Last season's 20-win squad — featuring Michael Porter Jr. and a collection of underwhelming young role players — finished last in the league in scoring (105.9) and offensive rating.

Brooklyn Nets forward Julius Randle (30) drives to the basket against New York Knicks center Andre Drummond (0) on Monday, Nov. 2, 2026, in New York. IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect

This season, the Nets received a much-needed infusion of talent — two-time All-NBA selection Julius Randle and No. 6 overall pick Mikel Brown Jr., along with Mo Wagner and Keon Ellis — but the team has struggled to develop offensive chemistry.

Through seven games, the Nets (1-6) rank 29th in scoring (105.6), 28th in offensive rating, 29th in assist to turnover ratio (1.21), 28th in turnover percentage (18.3) and 28th in field goal percentage (41.7).

Entering Wednesday's game against the Hornets (3-5) — which may see second-year star Kon Knueppel make his season debut — Brooklyn is averaging 94 points over its past three games. In Monday's loss to the Knicks, the Nets scored a season-low 90 points, allowing a late lead to evaporate as they shot 3-for-16 with five turnovers, while scoring 11 points in the fourth quarter.

"I think it's more about us not being organized, and then if you have empty possessions, you don't run anything for anybody, like nobody's in the right spot," Fernández said. "You don't touch the paint. You don't move. You don't reverse the ball, and you get either no shots or terrible shots. … Everybody's got to do their jobs because whether we call a play or not, you got to run to your spots, and we didn't do it enough times, and that's the frustrating thing. When we do it, we get good results. When we don't do it, we get bad results.

Brooklyn Nets head coach Jordi Fernandez watches his team during the first half of an NBA basketball game against the New York Knicks, Monday, Nov. 2, 2026. AP Photo/Frank Franklin II

"We still gotta run more and find those easy ones. We're not there yet, but I think we're gonna keep working, keep watching it, and then we'll see good results. … The things that we didn't do as well in the fourth, I'm going to take responsibility and help them."

Randle is averaging a career-high 4.1 turnovers per game and shooting 41.5 percent from the field, well down from his career mark (47.2). Brown is shooting under 30 percent from the field in the first five games of his career. And the point guard spot has been split by a pair of 20-year-olds (Egor Dëmin, Nolan Traore).

Mikel Brown Jr. (0) of the Brooklyn Nets drives to the basket against the New York Knicks on Monday, Nov. 2, 2026, at Madison Square Garden in New York. NBAE via Getty Images

There has been bad spacing, poor ball movement and constant confusion. There is plenty of blame to go around.

"Just gotta remain disciplined," Randle said. "We know what we need to do … you can't just put it on one person. It's a team game. It's five players out there, so we got to be better at communicating, understanding the moment, what's going on. It's all five of us. We all got to be better out there."

#2740. The Day After the Day After: The Houston Texans resume their season after the bye

The Day After the Day After…when the raw, immediate emotions from the aftermath of a game diminish into the realm of clarity and the proverbial (or literal) hangover no longer haunts the mind. With that, a review of Houston's Bye Week:

Where does Houston stand vis-a-vis the league after the bye? While Houston took the week off, the chaos didn't stop. That will likely continue when Houston gets back to their schedule. When they kick-off next Sunday in LA, they will be no better than 2.5 games back of the Jaguars, possibly down 3.5 games. They still have three division games (all at home) left. As for a Wild Card, sitting 11th in the conference does not help their situation. They sit 2.5 games back of New England for the final spot, with Cleveland, Las Vegas and Baltimore still ahead of them. They have three remaining non-conference games, but all of those are on the road and in December/January. While they are a maddening 0-4 at home, they somehow have a winning road record at 2-1. Given that the remainder of the schedule is 6 road games/4 home games, that may not be the worst thing in the world. On the opposite end of the spectrum, Houston holds the 8th pick in the 2027 draft. Just based on numbers, Houston could remain in the draft top 10 if their struggles continue. If the franchise gets solid play from Stroud in spite of bad team play and decides to give him that second contract, it could make Houston game for some wheeling and dealing related to that draft pick.

The criticality of November: At 2-5, Houston finds themselves well back of the conference leaders. Still, there are 10 full games left. To be in legitimate position for a playoff berth, Houston will likely need at least double-digit wins. To get to the usual 10-7 record, Houston has to go 8-2. In particular, this squad can't go any worse than 3-1 in November. Arguably, that will need to be 4-0. On one hand, this past week offered Houston one of the best schedule hands it could have been dealt. The LA Chargers are a league worse 0-7 and are as hard broke as any team in the league. The Cleveland Browns have the best record of the November slate at 5-3, but Watson's play is falling off and they could possibly overlook the Texans, who will have a losing record when they go to Cleveland in two weeks. The Colts come to Houston, but they have been in fire-sale mode and might just be without long-time Texans' nemesis Jonathan Taylor when they play late in the month. The calendar ends with a visit from the usually nightmarish Baltimore Ravens, but after this weekend, when they lost their QB1 and QB2 for significant time, they might be in a weakened state.

On the other hand, all of that relies on Houston playing to its potential and not surrendering the explosive plays like they have. How often have golden paths been paved with fool's gold for this franchise? November takes on added significant due to those games being conference matchups, and upping that conference record is going to be critical for overcoming the slow start for the team if the playoffs are to happen.

Will the result on LA change anything for the Texans' roster? A win means the team can still hold out hope for a run. A loss? It doesn't mathematically eliminate the Texans, but for all intents and purposes, the team will be out of the running. That matchup will end under 48 hours from the trade deadline. Houston added Harrison and they likely aren't done talking with other teams. However, if Houston loses, do they start off-loading players to try to recoup for the offseason? Houston hasn't said as much, but especially if the squad can't overcome the worst team in the league, that would force some tough discussions on the flight back. As it stands, Houston doesn't have a lot of easily tradeable players. Sure, a player like Danielle Hunter would be on a lot of wish-lists, but how many teams could accommodate this contract and salary cap number? Maybe Xavier Hutchinson is traded not for an improvement, but for some draft capital for next season.

How much improvement can a bye really offer? In theory, a bye offers a chance to fix some issues. Yet teams only have a week. It is not like teams can engage in a full-up training camp and fix all the issues. Maybe they can throw in some new plays or adjust some facets of their strategy. Coaches can be fired and new personnel put it, but that doesn't always spark the desired change. The desperation firings of Chris Palmer as OC in 2005 did nothing to help that hapless offense and the sacking of Bill O'Brien in 2020 did not salvage that season.

Could Houston get flexed out of their prime-time slots? The schedule-makers back-loaded the Texans' primetime appearances, with a Week 11 Thursday Night game against the Colts, a Week 13 Sunday Night matchup against Pittsburgh, a Week 16 Christmas Eve duel against the Eagles and an Week 17 Monday Night game against the Packers. The Colts game is ineligible for flexing. The Christmas Eve game is also locked in, for better or worse. However, the Sunday Night Matchup at Pittsburgh and the Monday Night Game against Green Bay can get flexed. The league would need to give 12 days' notice and there would be a lot of horse-trading going between the networks. Much depends on Houston remaining in the playoff mix. Pittsburgh and Green Bay rest in playoff position and have rather strong fanbases that help ratings. However, if Houston is playing out the string by Thanksgiving, look for one or both of those games to get moved. The Texans did have one scheduled Sunday Night Game in 2013 flexed to an early afternoon kickoff (their home game against the New England Patriots).

1-2: Houston's record post-bye under Ryans. 2023 saw Houston exit a bye week only to lose an ugly matchup with a bad Panthers' team on the road. 2024 saw the team return from a late bye to beat the Dolphins to clinch the division at home after a Colts' loss later that day. Last season, Houston came off an earlier bye only to lose a tough Monday Night matchup at the eventual Super Bowl Champion's home in Seattle.

.703: Houston's post-bye winning percentage in the regular season during the Ryans' regime: Remember the whole 8-2 target? Well, it might not completely be out of the norm for a Ryans' squad. In 2023, the team exited it bye with that bad loss to Carolina but still finished the year 7-4. The late bye skews some of this, as Houston had a Week 14 bye before a 3-game stretch in 11 days, finished the year 2-2. Last season's 9-game win streak did most of the lifting for a 10-2 finish.

Given that there were no games or major news of note good or bad for players, we'll forgo awarding of game balls or declarations of idiocy. Those will resume next week.

The second part of the season starts in LA against the 0-7 Chargers. Kickoff is slated for 3:05 CST with coverage on CBS/Paramount+ (unless the game were [deservedly] flexed to local public access at 5:30 a.m. Sunday morning). See y'all there.
