#2736. Amanda Serrano and Skye Falzon Face Off In Puerto Rico

Seven-division world champion Amanda Serrano confirmed her final fight will take place on January 9 in Puerto Rico at a news conference Tuesday.

Serrano will face Skye Falzon of Australia in a 12-round fight with three-minute rounds in the main event of a Most Valuable Promotions card airing on DAZN Boxing.

Serrano will attempt to break Christy Martin's all-time knockout record in her final fight.

After 18 years as a professional boxer, seven-division world champion and trailblazer Amanda Serrano has nothing left to prove as she makes a beeline for the Boxing Hall of Fame. But she will shoot for one last goal in her farewell fight on January 9 at the Coliseo de Puerto Rico in San Juan.

Amanda Serrano arrives at the kickout press conference Tuesday in Puerto Rico announcing her retirement fight. Photo: Danny Mosaic, Most Valuable Promotions

The historic event will mark the final professional fight of seven-division world champion Amanda "The MOAT" (Most Of All Time) Serrano (50-4-1, 32 KOs), who will defend her unified WBO and WBA featherweight world titles against Australia's number four WBA contender Skye Falzon (12-2, 7 KOs).

Much like her longtime rival, Katie Taylor, Serrano will enjoy her last fight in front of her devoted fans on her island, a tribute she richly deserves, airing live on DAZN Boxing.

At Tuesday's kickoff event, Serrano and Falzon came face-to-face to discuss the highly anticipated showdown and the significance of Serrano's final fight.

Puerto Rico's first and only undisputed boxing world champion will close her legendary career in front of her home fans, continuing her fight for equality in women's boxing while seeking to break the all-time women's knockout record. Serrano and Falzon were joined by Most Valuable Promotions founders and co-CEOs Nakisa Bidarian and Jake Paul for the official fight announcement in San Juan.

"Back when MVP was just an idea and a promise to put fighters first, Amanda was the first athlete to believe in myself and my partner Jake Paul," recalled Bidarian. "She entrusted us with her career, And she convinced us to go all in on women's boxing.

"Before she even met us, she was a seven-division champion. And since she's met us, she's added more belts. She's become the first and only male or female undisputed champion in the history of Puerto Rico, she's fought for equality and choice for women in the sport of boxing, including giving up her WBC belt to take a stand for three-minute rounds. She's used her platform to push the next generation of male and female Puerto Rican boxers," said Bidarian, noting that her dedication over 18 years has brought her to her final fight, being called "The Last Walk."

"We get to witness the greatness of Amanda Serrano on the last walk to the boxing ring. It's going to be an incredibly loud and an incredibly emotional night, but above all, it will be a celebration of the most decorated boxer in the history of this great land," said Bidarian.

Amanda Serrano poses with opponent Skye Falzon and her Most Valuable Promotions team, Nakisa Bidarian and Jake Paul. Photo: Danny Mosaic, Most Valuable Promotions

Serrano has sold out venues from Madison Square Garden to AT&T Stadium. But she said she always knew her last fight would be in Puerto Rico.

"It means everything, and I always knew that my last fight, my last step will be here in Puerto Rico. You guys been with me from the very beginning, supporting me, loving me, and I've been fighting for you guys," saying her flag is always in her heart. "I just want you guys to celebrate my long journey, and it's gonna be a great night."

Serrano has made no secret of her quest to break Christy Martin's all-time knockout record. Currently, Serrano and Martin are tied with 32 knockouts. Serrano said it's why she made sure her last fight will be 12 three-minute rounds.

"I'm so thankful and grateful to Sky for taking the fight. I mean, she's a warrior too," said Serrano, pushing back on some naysayers who diminish Falzon as an opponent.

"She deserved this opportunity, and I know she's gonna come, and she's gonna try to come upset me here in Puerto Rico," declared Serrano. "But I'm gonna go out there, and I'm gonna give it my all. If the knockout comes, it comes. But I'm gonna enjoy every second of the last time I go into that ring. And you guys are gonna be in for a treat!"

Skye Falzon said she intends to seize the moment against Amanda Serrano. Photo: Danny Mosaic, Most Valuable Promotions

Falzon said she never imagined she'd get a call up to face Serrano.

"I'm a fan of hers. She is the best, and that's just the way it is. To get a call up to fight her was a dream come true," admitted she shed some tears when getting the offer . "The opportunity is something I'm gonna grab hold of, and I just can't wait.

"I've got a great team, and I have a great technical coach. All I got to do is listen and execute what he tells me to do," said Falzon. Falzon said fighting 12 three-minute rounds isn't daunting. She said she regularly trains three-minute rounds in the gym and will now implement them in her sparring.

Serrano said she knew it was time at 38 years old to end her groundbreaking career. But she will remain involved in her management role with MVP and says there is still work to do.

Amanda Serrano vowed to keep fighting for complete equality in women's professional boxing. Photo: Danny Mosaic, Most Valuable Promotions

"The (sanctioning) organizations need to come together and still allow the women to fight the three minutes. I want people to remember me as the game changer, and I gave it my all in the ring. Every time I fall, every time I train, I just left everything in the ring, and I hope you guys see that when I do fight, and I hope you will see that come January 9.

"I'm part of a great team that continues to change the game, and I'm so thankful and blessed.'

When asked what would change if she wins on January 9, Falzon politely pushed back, saying, "Did you say 'if' I win? When I do win on January the ninth, it will be game-changing for me. For everything I've worked for. It's just a dream. If you can't dream it, then you can't achieve it.

"I'm not here just to take part in Amanda's history. You know, I'm here to try to write my own, and I wouldn't be a fighter if I didn't believe I could win," insisted Falzon.

Just like Flora Pili of France who stepped up against Katie Taylor in her final fight, a great champion requires a solid opponent giving her all to create a memorable event. Serrano said that's exactly the way she wants it.

"It's beautiful, and I wouldn't like if any of my opponents will come thinking they're gonna come to lose, I love to fight the best out there. I love that she's gonna come in shape and she's gonna try to take my titles away. These titles are gonna stay here first and foremost. But I love and just for her to go with that mindset knows that when I do beat her, I'm beating the best, Skye Falzon."

Amanda Serrano was denied the all time women's knockout record in her August fight against Lecrecia Manzur of Argentina. Photo: Most Valuable Promotions

It's no secret Serrano is chasing the knockout record. She was denied the knockout in her August fight against Lecrecia Manzur of Argentina. She called it the 'cherry on top' if it comes, but said she will be concentrating on a final victory, and if the knockout comes, it's a bonus.

"I know Puerto Rico is gonna come out. You guys helped me to where I'm at right now, and this is our story. Not just my story, not just my journey. It's our journey, so I would love for you guys to come and celebrate this night with us … I'm gonna give you one last show!"

Asked whether she had a message for young girls and women aspiring to follow in Serrano's footsteps, Serrano said there's no dream too big. "I thought my dreams were big, and I've accomplished my dreams. I accomplished my goals.

"Just believe in yourself. That's all you have to do. Believe in yourself. Train hard. Fight hard in anything you do.

"For me, greatness requires sacrifice. I sacrificed my whole life to be great, and that's why I'm sitting here as one of the most, as some say. Believe in yourself and work hard, and anything and everything is possible," said Serrano.

Tickets go on sale Wednesday, November 4, at 10 a.m. AST (9 a.m. ET) at Ticketera.com for The Last Walk: Serrano vs. Falzon, taking place on Saturday, January 9, 2027, at Coliseo de Puerto Rico in San Juan.

#2734. Kawhi Leonard injury update: Raptors star finishes knee treatment but still out

Kawhi Leonard is headed back to Toronto. Getting back on the court is the next step.

The Raptors announced Tuesday, Nov. 3 that Leonard, 35, has completed treatment for swelling in his left knee and will begin the return-to-play process in Toronto. The team will update his progress in one week.

Leonard has missed five consecutive games. He felt something in the knee during pregame warmups Oct. 25 and was scratched from a loss to the Minnesota Timberwolves. An MRI showed no structural damage.

Coach Darko Rajakovic said Oct. 29 that Leonard was getting his treatment outside of Toronto. At the time, NBA insider Chris Haynes reported Leonard would miss at least three to four weeks. The Raptors didn't say Tuesday whether that window has changed.

Leonard already has injury history with the right knee. Leonard tore the ACL in his right knee in the 2021 NBA playoffs and the meniscus in the 2023 playoffs – both with the Los Angeles Clippers.

Toronto brought the two-time NBA Finals MVP back this offseason, sending Brandon Ingram, Gradey Dick and draft picks to Los Angeles. The deal was agreed to in late June, then sat until September while the NBA investigated the Clippers and Leonard for a salary cap circumvention scheme. The league fined Leonard $700,000. He signed a two-year, $115 million extension with Toronto soon after.

Leonard played in the Raptors' first two games, both wins. He averaged 19.5 points, 7.5 rebounds and 3.5 steals but shot just 32.4% from the field. Last season, he played 65 games for the Clippers and averaged 27.9 points.

The Raptors (4-3) are 2-3 without him. The next update is due Nov. 10.

#2732. Josh Jacobs needs to display more (or any) contrition

In May 2026, Packers running back Josh Jacobs crossed a line that should never be crossed. And neither he nor his representatives are acting accordingly in what should be an effort to seek redemption.

He pleaded no contest to battery of a woman. He's fighting in court to keep the video secret. He's responding to additional allegations through a strident statement from his lawyers attacking the accusers.

The most tone-deaf gesture of all came last Thursday night, when he celebrated a touchdown by pretending to wear, and to be released from, handcuffs.

His implausible explanation, which accused Prime Video of not showing enough of the celebration and attacked the media for interpreting the images with their lyin' eyes, was contradicted by the full video of the event.

That's not the way to play this. His no-contest plea is equivalent to saying, "I did it." He should be contrite. He should be apologetic. He should be seeking redemption.

The Packers continue to stand behind him, primarily because he's the best running back on the roster and they want to win games. Their reported interest in Colts running back Jonathan Taylor strongly suggests that, if the Packers could get Taylor, the support for Jacobs would immediately evaporate.

Here's the basic reality. If the Packers were to cut Jacobs, would anyone sign him? The Chiefs took plenty of heat last week for adding kicker Justin Tucker to the practice squad; they may not be inclined to give another second chance to a player whose arrival would compound the negative reaction to Tucker's arrival.

The reality, in every sport at every level, is obvious. If the player has enough skill and ability, someone will find a way to justify behavior that shouldn't be tolerated by an industry that relies so heavily on support from the public, both directly through ticket sales and TV ratings and indirectly through taxpayer funding for stadium projects.

Still, Jacobs has done himself no favors by adopting a posture of defiance. He did something no man should ever do. He's lucky he's good enough at football to not lose his job over it.

If he was at the bottom of the depth chart in Green Bay, he would have been gone a long time ago.

#2731. St. Joseph shuts out Ridgefield, claims second straight FCIAC girls soccer championship

FAIRFIELD - The FCIAC title on the line alone Tuesday night would have served as motivation enough for girls soccer teams St. Joseph and Ridgefield.

Both teams were looking to add another championship banner, having combined for 16 league titles. Neither team had lost a game coming in. And both teams play outstanding defense.

Both defenses were again on display at Tetreau-Davis Field. In the end, it was St. Joseph with the 2-0 shutout. Sophia Santorsola was the difference, scoring late in each half for the Cadets.

"I think we are the best defense in the state," St, Joseph goalkeeper Cailyn O'Hara said. "There's no argument about that. And we proved it."

St. Joseph has been No. 1 in the GametimeCT power rankings since defeating Greenwich in October. Ridgefield is currently third. St. Joseph is also No. 1 in the Class LL/L state coaches poll.

The teams played to a scoreless tie on Sept. 29.

It was the second-straight FCIAC tournament championship for the Cadets (16-0-2) and fourth in five years. St. Joseph has now appeared in the last five finals and has eight league titles overall.

So it remains the same: you still have to go through the Cadets to claim the FCIAC crown.

"People can hate us, people can hate me, but the bottom line is this: five straight years to the finals, four out of five years, we won it, and that's because of those players," St. Joseph coach Jack Nogueira said.

This was the 16th shutout for St. Joseph. O'Hara, who will play soccer at Sacred Heart University next season, allowed just two goals, one each to Trumbull and Greenwich, the latter on a penalty kick.

"This is a microcosm of what we've been all year," Nogueira said. "The ability to score goals when we need to and defend."

Ridgefield (15-1-3), which has 15 shutouts, allowed eight goals, including four to Greenwich in two games.

"I think we can use this experience, our first final in a few years, to hopefully learn from it, use it as motivation to go on a good state run," Ridgefield coach Barry O'Reilly said.

St. Joseph and Ridgefield are the top two seeds in the CIAC Class LL bracket.

Ridgefield tested O'Hara and the St. Joseph defense, but were not able to get the equalizer in the second half.

Meanwhile, Santorsola was able to notch her pair of goals. The first one came with 63 seconds left in the first half on an assist from Sara Wicker. Ridgefield goalkeeper Cathryn Mills got a hand on Wicker's shot, but she could not control it.

Santorsola then dumped it into the open net.

"I passed it to her (Wicker) first and she took her shot," Santorsola said. "I saw it come out, I knew I had to be there for the rebound. Second goal, I knew there was not much time left, but I saw the opportunity and I just took it."

Santorsola's second goal came with 1:09 left in the game.

"The FCIAC is definitely so full of a lot of talent," O'Hara said. "Props to Ridgefield, I think they're an amazing team and they gave us a bit of a run for our money. But to be able to go back to back is something to be honored and looked at."

The sophomore scored both goals for the Cadets, both late in each half.

"Sophia does what Sophia does for us, she pressures the ball, she's all over the field and has an innate ability to find garbage goals. That's no disrespect to her because a lot of people made a lot of money scoring garbage goals." - St. Joseph girls soccer coach Jack Nogueira

#2729. NBA rescinds Luka Dončić's technical foul during win over Heat, bringing him back to 1 on the season

Luka Dončić's latest technical foul has been called off.

The league rescinded a technical foul the Los Angeles Lakers star picked up during LA's 138-117 win over the Miami Heat on Monday night. The foul, which Dončić earned in the second quarter at Crypto.com Arena, was reviewed by the league Tuesday.

That has brought Dončić to a single technical foul in eight games this season.

The incident Monday happened after Dončić reacted to a call an official made, which led to a candid conversation between Dončić and the officials on the broadcast.

"I clapped. That's a technical? Come on now," Dončić told the official. "If it was anybody else, you know it's not a technical. Come on now."

Klay Thompson hit the free throw after the technical, which brought the Heat within five points at the time.

Dončić was asked about the technical after the game, but he declined to get into it.

Dončić finished with 42 points, 13 assists and 7 rebounds in the win. He's averaged 43.4 points per game over the last five outings, which included a 52-point night against the Utah Jazz on Oct. 25.

Dončić has had issues with technical fouls. He was suspended for a game last season after reaching the 16-technical foul threshold, which triggers an automatic one-game suspension. He had three straight seasons with 15 technical fouls each, and 13 during the 2024-25 campaign.

Two players in the league already have three technical fouls this season. Golden State star Draymond Green is one of them after he was ejected Monday night for an incident during the Warriors' win over the Phoenix Suns. Houston's Jabari Smith Jr. also has three.

It's still very early in the regular season, and Dončić has a long way to go before having to worry about such a penalty again. But having Monday's rescinded undoubtedly gives him extra room to work with down the stretch.

#2728. How confident are you in the Bears and in Caleb Williams moving forward?

Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NFL. Throughout the year, we ask questions of the most plugged-in Bears fans and fans across the country.

The Chicago Bears have won three straight games in the most impressive fashion imaginable. Caleb Williams is the 1st quarterback in Bears history to lead his team to 30+ points in three consecutive games with no turnovers. The Bears also never trailed in any of these three games, and that 3-game streak of scoring 30 points while never trailing is tied for the second-longest streak in franchise history. They went four in a row three times, all in the 1940s (1941, 1942, and 1948). Those teams were led by Hall of Fame quarterback Sid Luckman, who is the only quarterback to win a league MVP for the Bears.

There was some buzz around Williams as an MVP candidate before the season, and that was amplified following the Bears' 59-point explosion in Week 1, but the hamstring injury seemed to derail that because it kept him out of the next three games.

In his weekly NFL MVP Tracker at NFL.com, Kevin Patra wrote about the historical unlikelihood of Williams winning it.

In the post NFL-AFL merger era (since 1970) in non-strike-shortened seasons, only one player has missed three games and still won the NFL MVP award: Joe Montana in 1989. Cool Joe battled through various injuries that season, missing Weeks 6, 8, and 15, and portions of others.

While a long shot, the Bears did just beat last year's Super Bowl participants in back-to-back weeks on primetime. They also have three more stand-alone games on the schedule, including a third straight primetime affair this Sunday.

Patra also explained why Montana's performance in 1989 won it that year and how Caleb could have a similar path.

Despite missing three games, Montana was the best QB on the best team in the NFL, winning the MVP vote in a landslide (62 of 70 votes). The 49ers QB overcame the lack of counting stats by leading the NFL in all the efficiency categories: 70.2 percent completion rate, a 6.7 TD% rate, 53.7% success rate, 9.1 yards per attempt average, 270.8 yards per game, and set the then-record with a 112.4 passer rating — when 100 passer ratings were uncommon.

That's Williams' path to the MVP: Be the most efficient passer on the best team.

Caleb may not hit gaudy passing yard or touchdown numbers, but if all his other numbers are among the best in the NFL, while the Bears keep winning games, how could he not be a finalist?

#2727. Avalanche sign star Cale Makar to largest contract in NHL history at $163.2 million

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

This has been the summer of spending in the NHL, and the Colorado Avalanche just broke the bank for star defenseman Cale Makar. On Friday, the team announced that Makar signed an eight-year extension worth $163.2 million.

The contract is the richest in league history -- both in total value and annual value at $20.4 million per year. Makar is the first player in NHL history to cross the $20 million salary threshold.

At 27-years old, Makar is arguably the best defensemen in the NHL, and he will remain in that conversation for quite a while. Makar has already won the Norris Trophy twice, and he was a key factor in Colorado's Stanley Cup run, which ended with him winning the Conn Smythe Trophy.

This past season, Makar posted monster numbers from the blue line yet again as he tallied 20 goals and 59 assists in 75 games. Since entering the NHL in 2019, Makar leads all defensemen in goals (20) and points (507).

"I am so excited and humbled to continue to wear the Avalanche sweater and represent this incredible organization and community," Makar said in a statement. "I would like to thank the Kroenke family, Joe Sakic and the entire Avalanche organization for their commitment, trust and belief in me. I would also like to thank my wife and family for their constant support, as well as Scott, Brian and Steve Bartlett for their guidance and assistance.

"To the Avalanche fans, thank you for your continued support and for welcoming us to Colorado years ago. Colorado has truly become a second home to us, and we are so grateful to be here. I look forward to getting back on the ice with my teammates and continuing to work toward our goal of bringing the Stanley Cup back to the Mile High City."

Over the last three seasons, Makar's impact has been immense in all three zones. He's posted a five-on-five expected goals share of 54.5%, per Natural Stat Trick. With Makar on the ice in those situations, Colorado has outscored its opponents 220-157. In two of the last three seasons, Makar has hit the 90-point mark, and he has 100-point potential at his best.

Makar's $11.4 million raise kicks in in at the start of the 2026-27 season, and it will make things significantly tighter for the Avalanche as they navigate the salary cap. The bright side for Colorado -- and the key in getting this deal done -- is that the team now has each of its core players signed through at least 2031.

There may be some sticker shock upon seeing the $20.4 million average annual value, but that's the new reality in the NHL as the cap rises exponentially. The previous record for highest salary in NHL history was just set earlier this offseason when the Anaheim Ducks signed center Leo Carlsson to a contract worth $18 million per year, and the Chicago Blackhawks announced a $75 million extension for Connor Bedard.

The next domino to fall will be an extension for Minnesota Wild defenseman Quinn Hughes, who is neck-and-neck with Makar as the best defensemen in the world. Waiting until after the Makar deal was announced to sign Hughes could prove to be a mistake for Wild general manager Bill Guerin.

#2726. Bills reverse course on "high-maintenance" C.J. Gardner-Johnson

The Bills said they’d be keeping safety C.J. Gardner-Johnson. And now they’re not.

Tuesday’s surprise move to release the veteran defensive back directly contradicts the comments made publicly by coach Joe Brady, on the same day Gardner-Johnson received a one-game suspension for spitting on an opponent during the Week 6 game against the Raiders.

“Look, C.J.'s a member of the Buffalo Bills,” Brady said on October 19. “We brought him here for a reason, and we know that he knows that he has to play better. He knows he has to be better for this team, and, you know, just like everybody else, right, we’ve got to learn from this stuff, and we have to improve and find ways to get better as the season goes.”

As one source explained it to PFT, the Bills decided that Gardner-Johnson was simply too “high-maintenance” — and that the talent and production didn’t justify the headaches.

Plenty of other teams could have told the Bills what would happen. Gardner-Johnson has hopscotched around the league, from the Saints to the Eagles to the Lions to the Eagles (again) to the Texans to the Ravens to the Bears to the Bills.

He has been good enough to get more chances, but not good enough to keep him around in light of the issues that he brings with him.

The Bills hoped to harness his attitude in order to give the defense a lift. In the end, however, the baggage outweighed the boost.

And now Gardner-Johnson becomes a free agent again. Plenty of coaches believe they can be the one to speak to a player’s better angels. As to Gardner-Johnson, the demons have won, far too often.

#2725. 2026 NHL free agent tracker: Patrick Kane returns to Blackhawks on two-year contract

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

NHL free agency has slowed down in late July, but some notable names are still coming off the board. Most notably, Patrick Kane is returning to the Chicago Blackhawks on a two-year contract worth $16 million, the team announced on Thursday.

Already a Chicago legend and future Hall of Famer, Kane won three Stanley Cups and a slew of individual awards with the franchise that selected him with the No. 1 overall pick in 2007. Kane's first stint with the Blackhawks lasted 16 seasons, and he piled up 446 goals and 779 assists in 1,161 games. Kane ranks inside the top five of just about every statistical category in franchise history, and he will get the chance to keep climbing those lists over the next two years.

The Blackhawks sent Kane to the New York Rangers at the 2023 NHL trade deadline, and he played just 19 regular season games there before hitting free agency the next summer. Hip surgery delayed Kane's decision until November of that year, but he ultimately landed with the Detroit Red Wings, where he's spent the last three seasons.

Last season was Kane's best with Detroit, and it proved that he still had some gas left in the tank, at least offensively. Kane posted 16 goals and 41 assists in 67 games -- with 19 of those points coming on the power play.

In his second stint with the Blackhawks, Kane will add another level of playmaking to the power play, and he should strengthen a top six forward group that's bereft of proven talent. Kane will also be an excellent mentor and sounding board for fellow No. 1 overall pick, Connor Bedard, who is set to miss the first month of the season after undergoing shoulder surgery.

Kane isn't the player he once was, but he'll give Chicago a bit more pop at the top of the lineup, and his first game back in a Blackhawks jersey will be a huge night for the city.

#2724. Another Gauthier hat trick, Ducks hot power play payback Canucks

VANCOUVER, B.C. – Last Tuesday in Anaheim, it was an "unacceptable," "terrible" and "careless" collapse to the last-in-the-league Vancouver Canucks.

This Tuesday in Vancouver, there was another offensive surge, and despite a push from the hometown Canucks, the Anaheim Ducks rode history to a payback victory.

Cutter Gauthier became the first player in Ducks history to net hat tricks in back to back games, as Anaheim's historically hot power play unit buoyed a 5-4 road victory at Rogers Arena on Tuesday.

Anaheim (7-7-1, 15 points) has scored 29 goals in the last five games and is 10 for 12 on the power play in the last three games. Ducks are the 10th team in NHL history to score three power play goals in three straight games and the first since the then-Mighty Ducks did it in March 2006.

Anaheim's 10 power play goals in three games is the most in the NHL since the 2008-09 Minnesota Wild, and Gauthier is the first player in NHL history with multiple power play goals in three straight games.

Mikael Granlund opened the power play scoring, and after Vancouver evened on its own power play, Cutter Gauthier scored his first of two with the extra man. Leo Carlsson scored a shorthanded snipe for a 3-1 lead, and Gauthier's second gave the Ducks a 4-2 lead into the third period.

Gauthier ripped his third goal less than five minutes into the third period for his second consecutive hat trick and a 5-2 lead.

Gauthier has scored goals in just four games this season, but each one has been a multi-goal night. He is the only the second player in Ducks history with three straight multi-goal games, joining Paul Kariya in 2000-01.

Gauthier has eight goals in those last three games and is the first player age 22 or younger to do so since Patrik Laine in 1998 and just the second since Teemu Selanne in 1993.

Beckett Sennecke assisted on all three Gauthier goals for his first career four-assist game. He is the fourth Duck in the last decade to register a four-assist game joining Ryan Getzlaf, Corey Perry and Nikita Nesterenko.

Liam Ohgren scored the Canucks even-up power play goal, 1-1, and Linus Karlsson scored off a turnover to cut the Ducks lead to 3-2. Jake Debrusk scored on the power play and again at five-on-five in the third period to bring Vancouver back within one goal, 5-4.

Laurent Brossoit stopped 19 of 23 shots in his second straight start as a Duck since being called up from AHL San Diego. Kevin Lankinen made 17 saves for the Canucks.

Anaheim continues its three-game Western Canada road trip with the first half of a back-to-back in Edmonton on Thursday. The Ducks then play in Calgary on Saturday before returning home to host Pittsburgh next Sunday.

Anaheim will debut its Hometown Remix jersey on Sunday against the Penguins. The sweaters for that league-wide alternate uniform initiative were unveiled yesterday morning and resulted in the Ducks' most single-day jersey sales at the Anaheim team store since the inaugural Mighty Ducks jersey in 1993.

Nico Myatovic made his NHL debut on Tuesday. The Prince George, British Columbia native is the second player of Anaheim's 2023 draft class to play in the NHL following Leo Carlsson.

Myatovic was called up from AHL San Diego to fill in for AJ Greer, who was placed on injured reserve yesterday with an upper-body injury. Greer took a blindside hit late against Ottawa on Sunday and did not return.

Jackson LaCombe earned an assist for the eighth straight game tying Francois Beauchemin for the second-longest such streak by a Ducks defenseman. Scott Neidermayer sits just one game ahead with a franchise-best nine-game streak.

Beckett Sennecke is the youngest player in Ducks history to record a four-assist game at 20 years, 279 days old. He beats out Ryan Getzlaf (20 years, 318 days) and Corey Perry (23 years, 168 days).

#2723. Josh Jacobs needs to display more (or any) contrition

In May 2026, Packers running back Josh Jacobs crossed a line that should never be crossed. And neither he nor his representatives are acting accordingly in what should be an effort to seek redemption.

He pleaded no contest to battery of a woman. He’s fighting in court to keep the video secret. He’s responding to additional allegations through a strident statement from his lawyers attacking the accusers.

The most tone-deaf gesture of all came last Thursday night, when he celebrated a touchdown by pretending to wear, and to be released from, handcuffs.

His implausible explanation, which accused Prime Video of not showing enough of the celebration and attacked the media for interpreting the images with their lyin’ eyes, was contradicted by the full video of the event.

That’s not the way to play this. His no-contest plea is equivalent to saying, “I did it.” He should be contrite. He should be apologetic. He should be seeking redemption.

The Packers continue to stand behind him, primarily because he’s the best running back on the roster and they want to win games. Their reported interest in Colts running back Jonathan Taylor strongly suggests that, if the Packers could get Taylor, the support for Jacobs would immediately evaporate.

Here’s the basic reality. If the Packers were to cut Jacobs, would anyone sign him? The Chiefs took plenty of heat last week for adding kicker Justin Tucker to the practice squad; they may not be inclined to give another second chance to a player whose arrival would compound the negative reaction to Tucker’s arrival.

The reality, in every sport at every level, is obvious. If the player has enough skill and ability, someone will find a way to justify behavior that shouldn’t be tolerated by an industry that relies so heavily on support from the public, both directly through ticket sales and TV ratings and indirectly through taxpayer funding for stadium projects.

Still, Jacobs has done himself no favors by adopting a posture of defiance. He did something no man should ever do. He’s lucky he’s good enough at football to not lose his job over it.

If he was at the bottom of the depth chart in Green Bay, he would have been gone a long time ago.

#2721. Vic Fangio: J.J. McCarthy was a "steal" for the Giants

In late September, the Vikings sent quarterback J.J. McCarthy — the tenth overall pick in the 2024 draft — to the Giants for only a fifth-round pick. And the Eagles, who are trying to end a six-game losing streak, have to deal with McCarthy on Sunday.

On Tuesday, Eagles defensive coordinator Vic Fangio addressed the various changes the Giants have made since last season, capped by his take on the Giants landing McCarthy to replace Jaxson Dart, who’s out for the year with a knee injury suffered in Week 2.

“They’ve got a really good offense,” Fangio told reporters. “They’ve got skill at the receiving position. They did a nice job raiding the Ravens, not only for John [Harbaugh], but for [tight end Isaiah] Likely and [fullback Patrick] Ricard. They’ve got a lot of the Ravens type offense that they had when [New York Giants senior offensive assistant] Greg [Roman] was there, and they’ve intermixed Kansas City type passing in there with [offensive coordinator] Matt [Nagy]. They’ve got it going right now. They’ve got good wideouts, good tight ends, two good backs. The quarterback has come in, in a short period of time and really done a nice job, for them to get him for a sixth-round pick is a steal.”

It was a fifth-round pick, not a sixth-round. But it was still a steal.

The Giants were desperate for help at quarterback. The Vikings were, apparently, desperate to unload McCarthy. Desperate enough to take a fifth-round pick, even though the Vikings possibly would have needed him to play at some point this season.

The end result is that the tables have quickly turned, and that the Giants are now the top dogs while the Eagles are currently all alone in one of the weakest divisions in football. And the idea that the Eagles beating the Giants in Philadelphia would be viewed as an upset says it all.

#2719. 3 tall hurdles the Mavericks have to jump when they visit the rival San Antonio Spurs

The Dallas Mavericks (4-3) no doubt have a bad taste in their mouths after Monday's 115-100 loss to the bottom-dwelling Sacramento Kings. And despite the San Antonio Spurs' own stumbling start to the 2026-27 season, a trip to the Frost Bank Center may not be the easiest palate cleanser to swallow.

After back-to-back losses to start the year, San Antonio (5-2) has found its stride in five straight wins as all-universe life form Victor Wembanyama has started to heat up, scoring 36 and 43 points in back-to-back games last week. He only had to play 24 minutes in the Spurs' 119-97 win over the Utah Jazz on Monday, which means he's been resting up for the matchup against the Mavericks since sometime in the third quarter, close to a full 48 hours before Wednesday's tip. The Spurs host the rival Mavs at 8:30 p.m. on Wednesday.

Here are three giant obstacles the Mavs will have to climb in order to get a win against last year's NBA Finalists from the Western Conference.

We're just 10 days removed, as of this writing, from the season's first matchup between the Spurs and the Mavericks, San Antonio suffocated Dallas, which was without second-year superstar Cooper Flagg do to a shoulder injury, 122-106, in that one.

Without Flagg, who was nursing a shoulder injury, and with Kyrie Irving sitting out suffering from "injury management" on the second night of the first back-to-back set of the season, the young Spaniard Sergio de Larrea took the reins for the Mavericks and turned heads for 21 points on 9-of-15 shooting (3-of-4 from 3-point range) in just his third-ever NBA game. The undermanned Dallas bunch kept it close for three quarters before San Antonio put the Mavs away late behind a balanced effort that saw Wembanyama score a game-high 23 points and Dylan Harper add 22 more.

The Mavs will show the Spurs a completely different look this time around, with Flagg and Irving fully operational for the marquee matchup. Irving was taken off the injury report after sitting out his second game of the year against the Kings. The pair combined for 68 points in the last game they appeared in together, last week's surprise 116-111 win over the Houston Rockets.

There's nothing figurative about the next tall hurdle the Mavs will have to get over (or through) if they want to get an ever-elusive win in San Antonio. They'll have to contain Wembanyama.

His 23 points, seven rebounds and four blocked shots in the teams' first meeting is a pretty good reference point. In that one, it wasn't really Wemby who overwhelmed the Mavs as much as it was the trio of swingmen in De'Aaron Fox, Stephon Castle and Dylan Harper, who got anything they wanted against Dallas "swinging door" defense.

Daniel Gafford will no doubt be instrumental in Dallas' effort to rein Wembanyama in on Wednesday. He's strung together two really good games, is averaging 1.9 blocked shots of his own so far this season and has pulled down seven or more rebounds in five of the team's first seven outings — the last five, actually. He's been much more effective and efficient than he was last season, when he was hampered by nagging injuries throughout the year. He's been an important cog while the Mavs wait on the rest of the tall tall trees, in Dereck Lively II and Santi Aldama, to get healthy.

Aldama is close, inching ever closer to making his Mavericks debut, as his progress on the injury report suggests. He has been upgraded to questionable for Wednesday's game as of Tuesday night. But for now, the tall task of limiting Wembanyama falls primarily on the shoulders of Gafford, who stands at least six inches shorter than the Frenchman.

Let's see how many bodies the Mavericks throw in Wemby's direction on Wednesday.

After yet another "injury management" related absence in what ended up devolving into an embarrassing loss to Sad Sack Sacramento, Kyrie Irving is not listed on the Mavericks' injury report going into the matchup against the Spurs. He needs to be the catalyst on offense at San Antonio — not to make up for the loss his absence could have prevented, no. But because when he's the catalyst on offense, the Mavs have a chance to take down even the league's better constructed teams.

Friday's win over the Rockets is just the latest evidence. The Mavericks don't have another player on the roster who can do the things that Irving can do — namely, dribble the basketball. He'll be the best-rested guest in the West, so there are no excuses, either.

In order for the Mavs to have a big night, it starts with a big night from the point guard position. Look for Irving ot log at least as many minutes (35) as he did against Houston and for the Mavericks to make this one a nail-biter down the stretch because of his disruption.

The Mavericks and the Spurs will tip off on Wednesday at 8:30 p.m. The game will be televised on ESPN, which means tip-off probably won't be until about 8:50 in reality. You can catch the stream on MavsTV, and the radio broadcast will be on KRLD 105.3 The Fan.

#2718. 2026-27 NHL season predictions: Expert picks for Stanley Cup playoffs, champion and major awards this season

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Following a brief offseason and an expedited preseason, the 2026-27 NHL season has arrived. Before the puck drops on opening night, we have some predictions to make.

If this season feel like it's staring earlier than usual, that's because it is. The NHL is adopting an 84-game regular season, which just means more hockey for the rest of us. That also means a long and arduous journey to the Stanley Cup is ever so slightly more difficult.

So, what will that journey look like? The Carolina Hurricanes are looking to defend their title as Cup champions, but they'll have to contend with a deep Eastern Conference and some real juggernauts in the Western Conference. With that in mind, we logged our expert predictions for the playoff field in each conference -- and there were a few surprises -- before making our Stanley Cup Final selections.

We also called our shot on the winners of each major individual award. Connor McDavid is looking for his fourth Hart Trophy, but he's got some competition from an up-and-coming superstar in his own division. Races for the Norris Trophy and Vezina Trophy should be pretty wide open, and unexpected candidates always emerge throughout the season.

It should be a fun season in the NHL, so follow along with all our coverage at CBS Sports. Let's get things kicked off with the season preview and predictions, which will of course be 100% accurate.

Baumgartner: I don't see many new faces entering the conversation when it comes to the Eastern Conference playoff race. A healthy Florida Panthers side will slot themselves right back towards the top of the Atlantic, and a revamped Washington Capitals side should be able to make some noise in the Metropolitan. Besides that, I have six 2026 playoff teams returning to the dance in 2027.

Nivison: As much as I hate to go with chalk in preseason predictions -- because it rarely happens that way -- there's no denying the top dogs in the West. The Avalanche and Stars are the class of the Central Division, and the Golden Knights should pound a pitiful Pacific Division into a pulp. Things get more interesting behind those clear Cup contenders, and I'm projecting another significant leap forward from the Mammoth. I also think Macklin Celebrini will be successful in dragging the Sharks to the playoffs in his third NHL season.

Nivison -- Columbus Blue Jackets: The Blue Jackets have been agonizingly close to the playoffs in each of the last two seasons, and I think they get over the hump in 2026-27. There are still questions in Columbus. Can Adam Fantilli be a franchise player at center? Is the forward group as a whole good enough to keep pace in a competitive Eastern Conference? Still, I am sure the Blue Jackets have a really strong blue line, led by Norris Trophy winner Zach Werenski, and goaltender Jet Greaves is on track to become a Vezina Trophy candidate. Internal improvements from the young core will then get Columbus above the cut line.

Baumgartner -- San Jose Sharks: The Sharks narrowly missed out on the 2026 Stanley Cup Playoffs, finishing just four points short of the second wild card. San Jose added a good group of veterans over the summer, but the most important offseason move was selecting Ivar Stenberg with the No. 2 pick in the Draft. Stenberg joins the youth movement in San Jose, which is spearheaded by new captain Macklin Celebrini, who broke the Sharks single-season points record with 115 last season. The Sharks are a better team than they were last year, and with Celebrini entering his third season as a legit Hart Trophy contender, this team won't be fun to play against.

Nivison: Yes, the Mammoth have a brutal path coming out of the Central Divison, but just close your eyes and imagine this scenario with me. Logan Cooley becomes a superstar center. Dylan Guenther hits 50 goals. Dmitry Simashev asserts himself as a budding top-four defenseman. Anders Lee and Vincent Trocheck provide necessary veteran depth. Now open your eyes. Utah is your Western Conference champion.

Unfortunately for the Mammoth, they will run into a refreshed Panthers team that now has double-barreled Tkachuks. Last season, we found out that all it takes to stop Florida is to hope all of its key players miss significant time with injury. The long offseason was probably a blessing in disguise as it allowed the Panthers to get healthy, and that's bad news for everyone else. The structure in front of the crease will limit some of the volatility we saw from Jacob Markstrom in New Jersey, and Florida wins its third Stanley Cup in four years.

Baumgartner: Before last season, the Carolina Hurricanes' kryptonite was the Eastern Conference Final. The Hurricanes were able to overcome their demons and win the East before ultimately taking home the franchise's first Stanley Cup since 2006. In the West, the Dallas Stars have been running into the same problem. After three straight seasons ending in the Western Conference Final, the Stars regressed last postseason, flaming out in the first-round to the Minnesota Wild. The Central Division will once again be a gauntlet, but I'm ready for Dallas to take the next step and reach the Stanley Cup Final.

While Dallas has continued to fall short in recent years, the Panthers have done the opposite. #2716. 2026 season could highlight the unfairness of the eight-division structure

From time to time, the NFL’s current structure has created unfair results, with the best of four bad teams assigned to a predetermined division earning a playoff berth and the home game that goes along with it.

This year, the NFC has two very strong divisions, one so-so division, and one very weak division.

Here’s the basic reality. With the four NFC division winners getting tickets to the playoff party, the wild-card berths will go to three teams. And, currently, there are three teams in the NFC North and two in the NFC West that are potentially better than whoever will win the NFC East and the NFC South.

Between the Vikings, Bears, Lions, Packers, 49ers, Seahawks, and Rams, two will be crowned division winners. That leaves five for the wild-card berths.

Ultimately, two of them will be frozen out of the playoffs — even if both of those teams end up with better records than the best teams of the NFC East and NFC South.

During last Friday’s episode of PFT Live, I threw out an alternative approach that would be far more fair to all teams.

Instead of two conferences with a quartet of four-team divisions, why not pivot to four eight-team divisions?

NFL East, NFL North, NFL South, NFL West. The easiest configuration would consist of slapping the current East, North, South, and West divisions into one conference each. While some tweaks could be needed to better align things geographically, it would be far more fair to guarantee a playoff spot (and a home game) to the best of eight teams, not the best of four teams.

Decisions would have to be made about scheduling. The home-and-home series (a vestige of the days when there were far fewer teams) would need to be retired. Each team would play the seven other teams in its conference, with 10 (or 11, inevitably) other games.

The playoffs would consist of the four conference champions (with the best two getting byes) and 10 wild-card teams. And there would be an added benefit — it would be possble to have the best two teams meet in the Super Bowl, without regard to the traditional AFL-NFL/AFC-NFC separation.

It would be one league. One playoff tree. Any combination of teams would, in theory, be possible for the Super Bowl. When the dust settles on the semifinal round, the best two teams would remain.

That said, it won’t be easy to get the owners to give up the current format, which entails in any given year a one-in-four shot at hosting a playoff game. But if the goal is to constantly strive for ways to create more compelling matchups, an eight-team, four-conference approach makes a lot more sense than the current structure.

Football is a meritocracy. A configuration of four, eight-team conferences would be far more conducive to that ideal.

Will it happen? Probably not. Should it be taken seriously by the league? Absolutely.

Maybe this year, when the NFC East and NFC South provide none-of-the-above champions and two very viable teams are sent home after Week 18, will spark a real conversation about meaningful change.

#2709. Doom and Gloom: Overreactions to Utah’s slow start to the 2026-27 season

This has not gone as well as we had hoped. Seven games into the season, and all that the "winning time" Utah Jazz are bringing to show and tell is a solitary one-point win against a subpar New Orleans team and a head bowed in shame. It was a depressing show-and-tell presentation for this premature Jazz team.

But growing pains are part of the deal. Winning in the NBA isn't as simple as a change in mindset; it's a change in identity. A fundamental shift in the direction of a franchise will take time to set, especially one as drastic as going from hunting the number-one overall lottery odds to walking the thorn-riddled path toward the Western Conference playoffs.

Just as Michael Scott learned that it takes much more than shouting in the office to declare bankruptcy, Utah is learning firsthand that flipping the "winning" switch is much harder than simply making a declaration. The Jazz wanted and expected to win many more basketball games this season; they clearly still have some growing up to do before they can reach that switch.

Still, it wasn't ridiculous to expect more from this team by now. They traded for Jaren Jackson Jr., one of the best front-court defenders in basketball and a multiple-time All-Star, to pair alongside Utah's in-house All-Star, Lauri Markkanen. They drafted Darryn Peterson, a player touted as one of the best guard prospects in recent memory and a future star. They re-signed Keyonte George, rewarding him for his steady growth and remarkable leadership.

But 1-6 is 1-6, and the Utah Jazz are way off course at this larval moment in the 2026-27 season. Not all is lost, but much needs evaluation and careful reconsideration. So let's play a game that I like to call "Doom and Gloom". The rules are simple: I'll share an opinion that I've thought myself or heard from others about Utah's unsettling beginning and determine whether said opinion is "Doom", a bad omen and an imminent issue, or "Gloom", an overreaction that, while based in reality, doesn't tell the whole story.

SAN ANTONIO, TX – NOVEMBER 2: Ace Bailey #19 of the Utah Jazz drives to the basket during the game against the San Antonio Spurs on November 2, 2026 at Frost Bank Center in San Antonio, Texas. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and/or using this Photograph, user is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. Mandatory Copyright Notice: Copyright 2026 NBAE (Photo by Adam Hagy/NBAE via Getty Images) | NBAE via Getty Images

No, the Utah Jazz are not winning basketball games. Yes, that is a massive problem, and a legitimate cause for concern for a team whose goal is to win basketball games.

But this problem, as with all others, deserves some context before it stirs up panic.

The biggest factor, I believe, is the Jazz's strength of competition. According to ESPN's RPI, the Jazz are tied at number-one for the hardest schedule in the entire NBA. They've faced the reigning Western Conference champions, San Antonio, twice while the Spurs were at full strength. Who could have foreseen the Memphis Grizzlies, who Utah faced twice, starting the season at 6-1? In fact, all the teams that beat the Jazz at this point of the season are a collective 22-6.

Despite the majority of this Jazz core having played together for years, this is a team still discovering itself. Give them time.

Injury luck has not flipped in Utah's favor early — five big men have been injured at some point in the season — but to blame their shortcomings on injuries is disingenuous.

Jusuf Nurkic hasn't been available since the first game of the preseason, Jaxon Hayes went down with an injury against Los Angeles, and then Markkanen and JJJ went down in the same half against Memphis. Markkanen and Hayes returned quickly, but shortly thereafter Mo Bamba — who has been unironically excellent — rolled his ankle in San Antonio.

That's bad luck, and Utah will obviously underperform without their best players on the court. But playoff-caliber teams regroup and find ways to win while shorthanded. If the Jazz can't win while JJJ recovers from his MCL injury, their playoff chances were slim from the start.

Alright, it's time for some therapeutic pessimism. On the topic of Utah's young players, I have to be painfully honest: Utah's tanking-fueled draft yield has been tragic.

Let's look at the Jazz's body of work in terms of draft picks. Of their four lottery picks, only two are still on Utah's roster. First to leave was Taylor Hendricks, who spends his days at the end of Memphis' bench and doesn't appear likely to sign an extension at the end of the season. It's a similar story for Cody Williams, who, despite generating plenty of preseason static in Minnesota, has appeared in five games and scored zero points.

Utah traded up to pick Florida star Walter Clayton Jr. last year, and he's already on his third NBA team.

As for the draftees still on Utah's roster, Isaiah Collier's team option was just declined, and Kyle Filipowski hardly sees the court even as injuries pile up in Will Hardy's frontcourt rotation.

Sensabaugh's minutes have been uneven, but he's filled his role well and had the trust of his head coach to replace Darryn Peterson in the lineup when their first clash with San Antonio entered overtime. Still, his status with the team is uncertain as he approaches the final year of his contract.

That list doesn't inspire much optimism, but it isn't all bad in terms of the youth of Utah.

Keyonte George has been excellent this year, with the exception of a stinker against San Antonio. Ace Bailey is a revelation, making winning plays with and without the basketball, playing stellar defense, and becoming an offensive rebound magnet. And Darryn Peterson, despite looking uneven out of the gate (more on this later), has still shown flashes of what makes him such an enticing prospect.

Semi-Doom is a bit of a cop-out, I'll admit. But there's still reason to believe in Utah's young core, even if the majority of their swings have inarguably whiffed.

Even worse than seeing Utah lose five consecutive games is seeing how the team has responded to adversity.

Without a rallying cry or an increased sense of urgency, this team is full of players with no experience winning at an NBA level. They haven't been able to hit that next gear, and the team mopes on the court, on the sideline, and in timeouts.

This is all about perception, so I might be out of line, but winners turn losing streaks into winning streaks. Utah is giving its fanbase little reason to expect a turnaround because they don't appear to expect one themselves.

Being a guard in the NBA is incredibly difficult, and development isn't linear.

What we're seeing in Peterson isn't a lack of basketball talent, ability, or confidence. In fact, he's displayed all three of those qualities in droves in his young career. Instead, we're observing the metamorphosis of a college star into an NBA-level player. Darryn Peterson joins a Utah Jazz team where he is the fourth offensive option behind Markkanen, George, and Jackson Jr. Finding his place in the rotation and getting accustomed to his new circumstances was bound to bring growing pains.

The biggest concern has been his lack of athletic burst and top-end speed, keeping him away from the basket. Instead, he's sustained himself on a diet of floaters and mid-range jumpers, while getting comfortable with a quick-trigger three-point shot.

For every poetic dribble combo leading into a buttery-smooth jumper, Peterson is due for a forced off-balance fling. He's playing in the big leagues, which means the competition is bigger, stronger, and faster than he's ever faced.

And I'm still highly encouraged by what he's displayed to this point. The jumper looks slick, comfortable, and will find its target with greater consistency over time. Keyonte was a sub-40% shooter from the field as a rookie; he shot 45.6% in his third year.

Alright, I'll wave the red flag for this one. Utah's offense has been abhorrent this season, and we can't blame tanking on their ratings anymore.

Currently possessing the 29th-ranked offense in the entire NBA, the Jazz have scored under 100 points in their last two games. Lauri Markkanen played in both of those games and has performed well beneath his standard. At just 16.5 points per game, the player who has been Utah's offensive pillar and averaged over 26 points per game a season ago is shooting below 40% from the field.

Against San Antonio on Monday, Markkanen and Peterson were the only Jazz players to score in double digits.

The absence of Jusuf Nurkic has been devastating to Will Hardy's offensive game plan. Heavily reliant on ball screens and passing from the center position, Jaxon Hayes simply isn't the playmaker this system requires to succeed. Nor are Mo Bamba or Tony Bradley.

Having to adjust on the fly, the Jazz offense has been clunky, ineffective, and overly dependent on self-creation to pose any real threat. Either one player's injury has truly been that catastrophic to Utah's offensive integrity, or Will Hardy is struggling to conjure up an alternative play style. Either way, none of this is good.

Calvin Barrett is the Associate Editor for SLC Dunk and a Utah Jazz columnist for the Standard-Examiner. Originally from Springville, Utah, he currently writes from his desk in Japan.

#2706. Bill Simmons compares ‘insufferable’ Luka Doncic to Gordon Ramsay in latest rant

Luka Doncic is enjoying a historic start to the 2026-27 NBA season, but Bill Simmons isn't happy with one aspect of his game.

Luka Doncic and the Los Angeles Lakers have started the season winning six out of their first eight games. The Slovenian superstar has been playing on an unbelievable level, the numbers he is putting up are spectacular.

Through seven games, Luka is averaging 38.3 points, 8.0 rebounds, and 8.1 assists per game. He is doing this while shooting 50 percent from the field, 43 percent from three-point range, and 89 percent from the free throw line. Despite all this, Bill Simmons thinks the Lakers star is 'worse than ever'.

One of the big criticisms that Doncic has faced in his career is his approach with the referees. In the past, he has received many a technical foul for complaining too much or doing it in a disrespectful manner. Luka has been called out for this numerous times, and spoken about wanting to improve.

It seems that Simmons thinks that not only has Doncic not improved, he is apparently at his worst at the moment. He said as much during one of his latest podcasts, giving an unexpected analogy.

"I think the guy is brilliant, I think he's one of the best offensive players I've ever seen in my life," Simmons said. "And it's not a new take to say that his behaviour during games has been a little insufferable. I think this is the most insufferable he's ever been.

"I can't believe how he behaves for 2.5 hours at these games and I don't know one person who enjoys it. To me, it's like when you see those commercials of Gordon Ramsay. Like, these reality chefs who are just screaming at everybody in the kitchen and you're like, 'Man it would s*** to work for that guy.'

"That's Luka now in every game, he's just unhappy constantly with everybody. And if somebody talks s*** to him on the other team, now he's got to focus his rage on this… I'm just saying… I don't want to put him on the Big TV because I don't enjoy the process of watching him get those stats."

Many analysts have said similar things about Doncic in the past; Simmons certainly isn't sharing a take which is unheard of. However, to do so at a point when the LA superstar's game is speaking volumes more than any of his antics is a bit bizarre.

#2705. Lakers star Luka Dončić has second technical foul rescinded

Los Angeles Lakers star Luka Dončić has created a lot of attention this past week with his ability to score.

He's managed to produce a fast start for the Lakers and has positioned himself as an early candidate for MVP.

Dončić produced a double-double in a 138-117 victory over the Miami Heat at Crypto.com Arena on Nov. 2. He finished with 42 points, 13 assists and seven rebounds.

The point guard did receive a technical foul with 1:12 left in the second quarter. He was initially called for the technical foul for clapping in the direction of an official as he was disputing a "no-call."

It would've been his second technical foul of the season, but it was officially rescinded by the NBA on Tuesday. He will not have to pay the $2,000 fine.

"This season," Dončić told reporters on Oct. 21. "I'm trying to not get techs."

More: Luka Dončić's offense is carrying Lakers. Is LA too dependent on its 'showman'?

Dončić had received his first technical foul of the season during a game against the Golden State Warriors on Oct. 30.

If a player receives their 16th technical foul in a single season, they are automatically suspended for one game and fined $5,000.

#2703. Vic Fangio: J.J. McCarthy was a "steal" for the Giants

In late September, the Vikings sent quarterback J.J. McCarthy — the tenth overall pick in the 2024 draft — to the Giants for only a fifth-round pick. And the Eagles, who are trying to end a six-game losing streak, have to deal with McCarthy on Sunday.

On Tuesday, Eagles defensive coordinator Vic Fangio addressed the various changes the Giants have made since last season, capped by his take on the Giants landing McCarthy to replace Jaxson Dart, who's out for the year with a knee injury suffered in Week 2.

"They've got a really good offense," Fangio told reporters. "They've got skill at the receiving position. They did a nice job raiding the Ravens, not only for John [Harbaugh], but for [tight end Isaiah] Likely and [fullback Patrick] Ricard. They've got a lot of the Ravens type offense that they had when [New York Giants senior offensive assistant] Greg [Roman] was there, and they've intermixed Kansas City type passing in there with [offensive coordinator] Matt [Nagy]. They've got it going right now. They've got good wideouts, good tight ends, two good backs. The quarterback has come in, in a short period of time and really done a nice job, for them to get him for a sixth-round pick is a steal."

It was a fifth-round pick, not a sixth-round. But it was still a steal.

The Giants were desperate for help at quarterback. The Vikings were, apparently, desperate to unload McCarthy. Desperate enough to take a fifth-round pick, even though the Vikings possibly would have needed him to play at some point this season.

The end result is that the tables have quickly turned, and that the Giants are now the top dogs while the Eagles are currently all alone in one of the weakest divisions in football. And the idea that the Eagles beating the Giants in Philadelphia would be viewed as an upset says it all.

#2701. Alexander Ovechkin announces this will be his last NHL season: 'Let's have fun'

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Alex Ovechkin's 22nd NHL season will be his last, the Washington Capitals superstar announced on Monday."This is gonna be my last year," Ovechkin told his teammates in a video the Capitals posted to social media. "It's sad, but it is what it is. We have an unbelievable team this year. There are 82 games left. Let's make the playoffs, and let's have fun."

Ovechkin has already established himself as the greatest goal-scorer in hockey history with 929 tallies, and he still has 82 games to add to that total before he hangs up his skates.

The No. 1 overall pick in the 2004 NHL Draft, Ovechkin immediately established himself as a prolific scorer by notching 52 goals en route to winning the Calder Trophy as a rookie.

Since then, Ovechkin has won the Rocket Richard Trophy as the NHL's leading goal-scorer a record nine times. The Capitals legend's resume also features an Art Ross Trophy and three Hart Trophy wins.

The crowning achievement in Ovechkin's illustrious career is leading Washington to its first Stanley Cup in 2017-18. After coming up short in a number of postseasons prior to that, Ovechkin led all playoff performers with 15 goals and won the Conn Smythe Trophy as a result.

Following the 2025-26 season, there was speculation that Ovechkin could retire, but he signed an incentive-laden one-year deal with the Caps.Sensing that this could be Ovechkin's final season, the Capitals loaded up to give their franchise icon one more shot at the Stanley Cup. Washington signed former Buffalo Sabres winger Alex Tuch in free agency and acquired winger Jordan Kyrou from the St. Louis Blues via trade.

No team is as loaded on the wings as the Capitals, and they have one of the best rosters in the Metro Division. Washington has the ingredients to challenge the defending Cup champion Carolina Hurricanes and get Ovechkin one more ring before he rides off into the sunset.

#2699. NBA rumors: Injury-plagued Thunder eyeing player 'they've already had,' and one surging star makes most sense

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Last season, a total of 11 players gave the Oklahoma City Thunder at least 900 minutes of service. Three of those players now play for other teams: Lu Dort, Aaron Wiggins and Isaiah Joe. Two of them, Jalen Williams and Cason Wallace, have already suffered injuries that may end their seasons. Another, Alex Caruso, has a sprained ankle. For Wednesday's game against the Dallas Mavericks, Chet Holmgren is also out with right knee patellar tendinitis and Ajay Mitchell is questionable with a right ankle sprain.

In other words, most of Oklahoma City's core rotation from a year ago, aside from Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, is not available right now. Inevitably, that has sparked quite a bit of speculation. The Thunder are as asset-rich as any team in the NBA. They have the picks to go trade for a difference-maker and a roster spot to add a free agent. The question here is who, and on Wednesday, ESPN's Brian Windhorst stirred the pot with an intentionally cryptic rumor.

"And this is one thing that I've talked to executives about, and I don't mean to be cryptic, but I'm being cryptic," he said on his Hoop Collective podcast. "If you're going to, if they're going to acquire a player, it would not be a surprise if they acquire a player they've already had."

This makes plenty of sense on paper. The Thunder are very particular about their culture. Bringing in someone new is far riskier than reacquiring someone they already know, and given their asset surplus, they can afford to be picky. Given Windhorst's track record of cryptic reporting leading to seismic transactions, let's take a look around the league to see which former Thunder players, if any, make sense as reacquisition targets.

The Thunder traded Dort, Joe and Wiggins last offseason. Given how things have played out, Oklahoma City may regret doing so, and given this rumor cycle, fans will inevitably call for them to try to reacquire one of last season's core pieces. Alas, Dort, Joe and Wiggins are functionally not obtainable to the Thunder. The NBA does not allow teams to reacquire players they have traded until the following season. That means Dort, Joe and Wiggins are off limits for now.

There is a very narrow exception to this rule, but it is not likely to come up. If the player is traded a second time and then gets waived, the original team can re-sign him upon clearing waivers. This happened with Mike Conley and the Minnesota Timberwolves last season. Of course, no team is likely to waive Dort, Joe or Wiggins, so we should assume for the sake of argument that they are off the table.

The Thunder have been so well-run for so long that the NBA is now littered with extremely accomplished Thunder alumni. Of course, these players are, in most cases, either so expensive that they would be impractical for Oklahoma City's purposes or so vital to their existing teams that they likely are not functionally available. So let's roll through those players now:

The players listed above are all currently under contract with teams trying to win today. There are, however, quite a few famous Thunder alumni who are theoretically much more gettable. Four stand out:

A reporter asked general manager Sam Presti on Monday about potentially bringing back retired team legend Russell Westbrook. Presti gave a typical non-answer. Fans would certainly love to see Westbrook in a Thunder uniform again, but the question here is whether he'd be able to accept a small enough role for this to be worthwhile. Westbrook, who announced his retirement in August, is a high-usage player whose value is mostly derived from having the ball in his hands. His issues as a shooter are well-documented, and while he's capable of the sort of intense on-ball defense the Thunder prefer, he's never been consistent as a team defender. All in all, Westbrook is probably just too high-maintenance an addition given what the Thunder could expect out of a 37-year-old.

The point guard Westbrook was once traded for, Chris Paul, makes a bit more sense. He and Gilgeous-Alexander thrived together during the 2019-20 season. However, Paul fell off a cliff during his brief return to the Clippers last season, and he's a notoriously demanding locker-room presence. He's now 41 and has shown no interest in playing in the NBA again after announcing his retirement in February, so we can probably cross him off the list.

Here's a sneaky one: Victor Oladipo. He spent this offseason trying to fight his way back onto an NBA roster. The Sacramento Kings worked him out, but did not sign him. He has not played since the 2022-23 season, but is still only 34. The healthy version of him fit into Oklahoma City's defensive culture, and after several years out of the league, he'd likely be happy with any role the Thunder could offer him.

The only non-guard in this section: Al Horford. The Thunder, again, have plenty of front-court depth. If they did elect to trade one of their bigs for help elsewhere, though, Horford is still useful in a smaller role and the Golden State Warriors simply aren't competitive enough to turn away offers for players in their 40s. The Thunder have several trade exceptions big enough to fit Horford, and his salary is just below the $6.9 million in second-apron space they currently have available.

Any of these three players theoretically could have landed in one of the last two categories. For reasons I'll explain, I wanted to separate them:

George is more expensive than any player we've covered thus far. The only scenario in which this would make sense is one in which the Thunder trade Jalen Williams to Boston (along with a few other contracts, for the sake of legality). That, obviously, is enormously unlikely. It just isn't so crazy that it should be taken off the table altogether. The Celtics already showed a willingness to take a step back this season in the name of the longer view when they traded Jaylen Brown for George in the first place. The Thunder, however, have much more at stake this season given their impending financial cliff. George, with his player option, could actually help on that front by potentially renegotiating a slightly longer deal that suits the Thunder's needs. There would have to be draft picks going to Oklahoma City, and George would have to be willing to take a team-friendly contract that pays him less than Williams is due next season. But if you squint hard enough, you can see something that sort of makes sense here.

The Thunder traded Giddey in part because his shooting made him an iffy off-ball fit next to Gilgeous-Alexander. Well, Giddey has made at least 38% of his catch-and-shoot 3s since coming to Chicago. The Bulls have a new front office that didn't bring Giddey in, and he's struggled to start this season. That doesn't mean they'll give up on him, but it means he could be gettable at the right price. Alas, price is the biggest hurdle here. The Thunder have no obvious way to cobble together the $25 million in tradable salary they'd need to match Giddey's contract without incurring an untenable first-apron hard cap. This would have to be a part of something bigger we can't foresee, so it's unlikely, but if the Thunder do something surprising, there might be a pathway here.

The Thunder could fit him into the trade exception they have leftover from sending out Dort, though they'd have to shed money elsewhere to duck the second apron. Schröder would likely be gettable for second-round picks later in the season (especially if Charlotte rookie Christian Anderson shows he can handle real minutes), and he'd simply be a spare ball-handler on point-of-attack pest defensively. He wouldn't have a big role in Oklahoma City, but the Thunder know him and what he brings to the table. Truthfully, though, the Thunder would probably just prefer to stick with what they have... unless things get worse.

Alright, we've spent the bulk of this story writing about players who wouldn't fit. Let's talk about the players who could. There are two standouts here:

The Thunder ironically chose Dieng one selection ahead of Williams in the 2022 NBA Draft, but Williams outplayed him and Dieng could never find a role in a crowded Thunder rotation. That rotation is less crowded now, especially at forward, and Dieng took advantage of all of the extra playing time he got for the Milwaukee Bucks after the trade deadline last season. Dieng has held a much smaller role for the Bucks this season, so he's theoretically gettable. He can't be traded until Dec. 15 because he just signed a free agent contract, but the Thunder likely don't want to rush into a move anyway.

This is the likeliest big swing on the table for Oklahoma City, if any is even possible. Jerome is in the middle of a breakout season for the Memphis Grizzlies and could be well on his way to an All-Star selection. He's also 29, has serious durability concerns, and is functionally on an expiring contract considering his player option. If the Grizzlies view this as a flash in the pan, or a chance to sell high on someone they don't want to give a big contract to next summer, the Thunder could be their chance. His cap figure is only around $9 million, so he's very obtainable. His shooting makes him an easy fit on any roster, and the Thunder have quite a bit of experience managing the workloads of high-impact players with durability concerns like Alex Caruso.

Jerome is a bit duplicative of Ajay Mitchell, but beggars can't be choosers. If the Thunder have to reorient their roster more around offense to maintain this season's title window, they should do so. Oklahoma City has enough of a draft surplus to trade for even an expensive rental. The question simply comes down to whether or not the Grizzlies view Jerome as a long-term fixture or a pleasant surprise they're willing to cash out. The former is likelier, but we can't rule out the latter.

#2697. 10 fantasy data points you need to know for Week 9
